blog_personal_01_luna.text:
Potty trained in 10 days. First we tried 3 things that blew up spectacularly. 
 Our daughter, Maya (just turned 2 years 9 months on May 14) was in desperate need of a potty solution by June. Sticker charts (Maya didn't care). Naked freedom (3 rug puddles). A "nice" weekend approach that kept prompting Maya until she ran behind the couch when we even said toilet. 
 In a long weekend back in Sacramento, June 7-16, we broke the spell. We stopped treating it like a test for her to pass. We began treating it like a habit she could learn. 
 Day 1. We cut out diapers totally for the day. Got 6 pairs of cheap cotton undies. Let Maya pick the purple ones. We also had a little floor potty in the bathroom and a waterproof mat underneath. We calmly said "Potty time" every 45 minutes or so. No "Do you need to go?". If she didn't want to, no argument. Try again later. 
 The big thing was let her own it. She brought her own undies to the laundry. She flushed. She picked a single treasure box (temporary tattoo or cheap plastic animal under $2) after each potty time success. Puddles were dull and no big deal. "Pee goes in potty. Let's clean it up". No shame. No lecture. 
 Days 3-4 were brutal. 6 accidents on Monday. Even one at East Sacramento library. Thought of giving up but our pediatrician said be prepared for inconsistency for the first week. So, we pushed on. 
 By Day 6, Maya could go for 2 hours without accidents. Day 8, she said "I have to poop" and made it to the potty. Marathon victory! 
 We still did diapers for napping and at night. Night time dryness is a different developmental milestone. Day 10, she was now totally regular during the day. Even when we went to grocery store or McKinley Park. 
 The magic potion wasn't perfect. It was consistency. Fewer words. Realistic expectations. Let Maya feel like it was hers.

We tried letting her run around naked (three puddles in the rug, yikes). We tried a "kind" weekend approach. She was prompted SO MUCH that she started hiding behind the couch when we talked about the toilet. 
 Then we had a break through. 
 It was a long home weekend in Sacramento (June 7-16). Instead of thinking about potty training as something she had to pass, we changed the approach to thinking of it as a new habit she could learn. 
 Day 1 - zero diapers during the day. We bought 6 cheapy cotton underwear. I let Maya pick the purple ones. 
 We also added a mini potty in the bathroom on the floor. And a waterproof pad under it. 
 We calmly (this is key) stated "It's potty time" every 45 minutes. No, "Do you have to go" question. Just the statement. 
 If she said no, fine. We didn't push. We'd just try again later. 
 What really worked was that we let her own it. 
 She brought her own underwear to the laundry basket. She flushed the toilet by herself. When she successfully went, she could pick one small item out of a treasure box (usually a $2 or less plastic animal or temporary tattoo). 
 Accidental pees or poos were just kind of boring and ho-hum. "Pees go in the potty. Let's clean it up." No scolding. No lessons. 
 Days 3-4 were rough. Six accidents Monday. (Including one at East Sacramento library! Holy geez, I thought, I give up!) But our pediatrician said it's normal for the first week to be inconsistent. So we persisted. 
 By Day 6, she could go for two hours at a time without wetting. 
 Day 8, she declared "I gotta poop" and made it to the potty in time! We won the marathon! 
 We still used diapers for naps and nighttime because night dryness is a different milestone. 
 By Day 10, she was consistently using the potty during the day. (Including when we went to the grocery store. Or McKinley park.) 
 We didn't do it the right way. It just happened to work. We were consistent. We used fewer words. We had realistic expectations. We let her own the process.

blog_personal_03_glm.text:
Grading is better than billable hours - my first semester as a teacher

Last August I exited Hendricks & Cole after 14 years as a corporate lawyer to enter Room 214 at Roosevelt High School with my provisional teaching license and mountains of fear. In October, I turned 42 and didn't spend my birthday responding to email on my phone for the first time in 10 years.

Why did I do it?

2022 I defended a merger that axed 300 people in an 8,000 person town. I couldn't get it out of my head.

My sister (20 years teaching 4th grade in Duluth) said, "You're always doing math about how much things cost. Now do some math about how much they're worth."

So that's my first semester teaching 11th grade civics and one section of constitutional law (yep, we have that in the district).

I'm paid $52.4k. In 2019, I'd have made that by March.

But I've never, ever worked at my desk for dinner. And I stopped my migraine meds in November because (knock on wood) I didn't need them anymore.

Wow. I was humbled by the learning curve. After 12 years of Yale Law + Big Law, I really thought classroom management was just "leadership skills." It's not. It took me until the end of September to realize my 31 sophomores (3rd period class) would only calm down if I'd let Marcus start class with his "news of the day" summary. Now it's the best part of my day!

The worst week was the week of 10/16. I stayed late for parent teacher conferences and 6 parents (some suspiciously so) wanted to know why a lawyer would want *their kids*

I'm being honest: 'cause there's a girl in my 2nd period civics class named Priya and she asked me whether she can post TikTok under 1st Amendment protection and it's the best question I've heard in years.

Dec 20th was the last day of final exams. I closed the gradebook and 84% of my students passed. And I had one kid (Diego) tell me he wants to be a lawyer now.

I didn't cry. But I was close.

I still carry my bar card in my wallet. Some things take a while to break.

But tomorrow morning at 7:45 when the bell rings, I'll know exactly where I'd rather be.

blog_personal_05_sonnet.text:
Flew into Kansai on a Tuesday in October. Planned on no more than ¥15,000/day ($100ish). And decided Kyoto is one of the easier places for this kind of thing. Swap the taxi for the bike, Michelin star for tofu shop. 
 Day 1: Haikyu Hostel near Kyoto Station. Dorm bed: ¥3400/night. Buy ICOCA at station kiosk. Rent bike from hostel ¥800/day. Skip bus for biking. Kyoto is flat. Lots of bike lanes.  Breakfast: buy pastry + coffee at Lawson konbini. ¥450  Ride to Fushimi Inari before 8am. Avoid tour buses. Free entry. Walk up to Yotsutsuji overlook in 40 minutes. Lunch: eat standing at soba shop near shrine. ¥600 for kitsune soba. Afternoon: go to Tofuku-ji temple (¥500). See garden.  Rent a bike, ride to Gion. Walk around. Free. Hanamikoji St. Free. Check out Yasaka Shrine. Free.  Dinner: eat a bowl of ramen at a counter place in Pontocho. ¥900. Buy can of Asahi from vending machine. ¥150.  Spend: ~¥10200. Under budget. 
 Day 2: Don't eat hostel breakfast. Buy onigiri from konbini. ¥300.  Bikes to Arashiyama to see bamboo grove. Free. Best before 9am. You and creaking bamboo.  Visit temple next door: Tenryu-ji. ¥500. Pond garden. Good.  Walk across Togetsukyo Bridge. Cheap curry for lunch near station. ¥750.  Go for snacks at Nishiki Market early afternoon instead of eating a meal. Eat skewer. Squeeze some tamagoyaki. Maybe ¥1200 total. Enough for lunch and snack.  Late afternoon: go to Kiyomizu-dera. Best time to go, sunlight. ¥400.  Walk down Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka. Free. Best looking streets.  Last dinner: katsu curry. ¥1100 
 2 days/2 nights. ~¥19000 total. So basically had almost another full day of budget in bank by day 2.  How? Avoid crowds for temples. Means better time to go to avoid crowds (means avoid wanting to pay $$ for tea to escape crowds). Use bike instead of some transit budget.

Arrived Tuesday in October to Kansai on a ¥15,000/day ($100) budget. Departed thinking Kyoto is among the easier places to do this. Just replace cabs with bike and Michelin with tofu shops. 
 Day one: Arrived at Haikyu hostel near Kyoto station. ¥3,400/night for dorm bed. Got ICOCA card at station kiosk. Rent bike from hostel ¥800/day instead of buses. Kyoto is low elevation and has lots of bike lanes. 
 Breakfast:  pastry and coffee at Lawson konbini. ¥450 
 Ride out to Fushimi Inari before 8am to beat tour bus crowd. Free to enter. Can walk up to Yotsutsuji overlook in 40 minutes or so. 
 Lunch: standing soba place near shrine. ¥600 kitune soba. 
 Afternoon: Tofuku ji - ¥500 entry for garden. 
 Bike over to Gion. Just walk around. Free to wander Hanamikoji street. Peep into Yasaka shrine. Free. 
 Dinner: bowl of ramen at counter place in Pontocho. ¥900. Plus can of asahi from vending machine. ¥150 
 Total for day 1: ~10,200. Under budget. 
 Day two: Skip hostel breakfast. Buy onigiri from konbini. ¥300 
 Bike out to Arashiyama for bamboo. Free. Better to get there before 9am to have place to yourself. Can hear creaking of stalks. 
 Next door is Tenryu ji temple. ¥500. Worth it to see pond garden. 
 Walk over Togetsukyo bridge. 
 Cheap curry for lunch near station. ¥750 
 Early afternoon in Nishiki market. Graze. Don't eat at a place. One skewer here. Piece of tamagoyaki there. Probably 1.2k for enough to be lunch + snack. 
 Kiyomizu dera in late afternoon. ¥400 to enter. 
 Walk down through Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka. Free. Best looking streets in the city. 
 Last dinner: katsu curry. ¥1,100 
 2 days/2nights. Total ~19,000 
 So that's almost one day's budget extra by day 2. 
 It's not about being poor. It's about visiting temples early to avoid crowds. (This means before you're enticed to buy over-priced tea to avoid the crowds...) 
 Bike can save you half of your transport budget.

blog_personal_07_luna.text:
January 1, 2025, I removed FB and Instagram from my phone and swore off both for 6 months. No big announcement. Just told close friends and family: “text me”.

Unbelievably physical. Locked my phone for a coffee in line at blue bottle in Oakland. Reach for instagram. Wait, shit, no. The first week I probably unlocked my phone 30 times a day for no reason. February it was much less. Started carrying a paperback book around. Mainly novels. But also a gardening book that had been untouched on my nightstand since 2023.

The biggest effect was how much quieter my head was. I hadn’t realized how much I’d be comparing my average Tuesday to someone else’s curated holiday / kitchen remodel / career announcement. All the sudden I wasn’t feeling slightly off and behind in my life. I found myself remembering more of what I read and heard. Now that I wasn’t scrolling right before bed I was doing a solid 20 minutes of reading time with my daughter Maya. Read 5 chapter books with her from Jan - June.

I was afraid of missing big news. Of not staying connected. I missed a few birthdays. And realized some friendships were really only held together by the occasional like and story reply. But I had better conversations. Talked on the phone with my college friend Daniel in Chicago 2x. We hadn’t done that in years. Me and my sister started doing Sunday voice messages back and forth.

Coming back was the worst. July 1st. Reinstalled FB/insta. Thought I’d be refreshed and all disciplined. But I slid right back in. Three days in. Deleted it again. Decided FB would just live on my laptop for a few select family groups.

The 6 months off made me neither more productive nor enlightened. Just more aware of my choices and of what was making choices for me. I discovered I’m not that terribly missing social media. I do miss some people. Now I know to just reach out.

I didn’t become more productive or enlightened after 6 months sans socmedia. It just helped me pay attention to what I’m choosing. And being chosen. I realized I don’t really miss it all that much. I miss some people. Now I know to just reach out.

blog_personal_09_glm.text:
Baking Sourdough at 5,000 Feet (And Why My 30th Failed Loaf Was My Turning Point)

So I moved to Boulder, CO (from Chicago) last June. I figured I was a sourdough expert. This was 'Gerald', my starter, named after my grandpa. He's been making beautiful loaves for 2 years at sea level. First time I tried baking at 5,430 feet. Hockey puck that could double as a brick. And tasted like disappointment.

Loaves 1-8: gummy, brick center

Loaves 9-15: bottom burnt, middle undercooked.

By loaf 20 my husband Dave was like, 'why don't we just buy bread'. I was like HECK NO. I've come too far for this.

The thing no one tells you about baking at high altitude is that water boils at lower temp (202f instead of 212f), you have 17% less air pressure and dough rises FAST... then it falls back out of the sky. So my typical 4 hour bulk ferment at sea level was over-proofing my dough before I knew it. It just wasn't structurally sound.

By loaf 30, I called Flour Bakery in Denver. Got a baker on the phone, her name was Marta. She laughed at me (nicely) and gave me the magic bullet changes:

1. Less water. 8%ish less. So instead of 350g per 500g flour I went to 322g. High altitude dough is all about creating more structure. 2. Down to 2.5 hours for bulk instead of 4 hours. Stop watching the clock. 50% rise instead of doubling. 3. This one felt like sacrilege - less starter. From 100g to 75g to slow things down.

For baking. I went from 475f to 500f in Dutch oven for first 20 mins with lid on. Then dropped to 450f (without lid) for 22 mins instead of 25. You need to set that crust quick or the middle gets too expanded and falls.

Loaf 31, snowy Saturday. Jan. this year. Got some ear on that puppy that you could hang a picture off of. Crumb was open. Glossy. Tangy. Slightly. My kids (Mia, 7 and Owen, 4) who had been very nice about my failures up until then, cheered.

Moral of the story isn't hydration %. It's unlearning. I had to dismantle 2 years of 'I'm a Sourdough Guru' to adapt. Gerald and I are students. Again. Not a terrible place to be, really.

If you're baking over 4000 feet and it's not working out. You're not a bad starter. You're not a bad baker. Make the changes. Don't watch the clock. And keep going until you're past loaf 30.

"5,000 Feet and 30 Bread Failures: My Sourdough Story"

Moving from Chicago to Boulder last June, I was pretty confident I could bring my sourdough skills along. I had Gerald (my beloved sourdough starter named after my grandfather) and two years of beautiful loaves at sea level. Then came my first attempt at baking at 5430 ft. And out came what was essentially a puck of hockey-like density, brick-like texture, and a whole lot of disappointment.

From loaves 1 - 8 I had the gummy, dense middle. From 9 - 15 I had burnt bottoms and raw middles. By loaf #20 my husband Dave was politely suggesting we just buy bread. But no. I was too invested!

Here's the thing about baking at altitude that no one tells you. Water's lower boiling point (202F here vs 212F), about a 17% decrease in air pressure, and the fact that your dough will rise quickly, but then fall quickly. So what I was doing at sea level (4 hour bulk ferment) would mean the dough would overproof before I knew it. The dough couldn't support the structure.

After bread #30, I finally reached out to Flour Bakery in Denver and got on the phone with a baker named Marta and pleaded for help. She chuckled kindly. And shared with me what really made all the difference.

1) Decreased my water by approx 8%. So instead of 350g water for 500g of flour I was down to 322g water. Sourdough needs more structure at altitude, that's a given. 2) Decreased bulk ferment from 4 hours to 2.5 hours. No longer watching the clock. But instead looking for 50% rise rather than the traditional double in size. 3) (Now feeling a bit of sacrilege) Decreased my starter from 100g to 75g to slow things down a bit.

For baking I increased the temp of my dutch oven from 475F to 500F for the first 20 minutes with the lid on. Then down to 450F for the next 22 minutes (instead of 25) and with no lid. So that quick burst of heat lets the crust set, rather than having the inside over expand and then collapse.

Loaf #31 (cooked up on a snowy Saturday this past January) had an ear to hang a picture from! Open crumb, shiny, slightly tangy. My kiddos Mia (7) and Owen (4) who had politely endured my bread fails, cheered!

It wasn't so much the percentage of hydration that I learned, as it was about unlearning. I had two years of thinking I "knew what I was doing". Which needed to be undone to adapt. We're (Gerald and I) learners again and you know what? That's not so bad!

So if you're baking at altitude over 4000 feet and struggling, it's not your starter or you. Adjust, watch the dough rather than the clock. And get through #30.

blog_personal_11_sonnet.text:
I sent my first invoice on Oct 14th last year for $340 (for a blogpost about industrial water filtration that I knew nothing about 3 days before). Now, I've sent 118 more. This year I've made $38,240 from 27 clients. Before I compile the story, let's jot down what really happened.

What surprised me wasn't the number. It's who made what. 4 clients made $24k. Ledgerly (SaaS) gives me $1,400 every month for a newsletter and 2 blogposts. Dental marketing agency in Ohio sends me $600/week on time. 23 other clients (1 off landing pages, email sequences, $75 product description for a dog leash co.) made up the rest ($14k) and took probably 60% of my time. I didn't realize the difference between fixed costs and retainers until I graphed it out in July.

My mistakes

1) I gave a fintech client a flat rate of $2,200 for "website copy" without defining pages. By March (11 pages later), I was effectively making $9/hr. I had to finish it because I'd already committed to it.

2) Until my accountant Priya asked in April if I did estimated payments, I hadn't saved for taxes. By June 15th, I had to make a payment of $6,100. I took it from savings.

3) I worked with a client (supplement brand) for 5 months even though checks started coming 20-30 days late. I liked the work. By the time I let go of them in Aug, they owed me $1,900. I didn't collect all of it.

But still, it was worth it. I quit a $61k salary job in Sept last year. So $38,240 from scratch in 1 year while learning all of the above is a number I'll take. Year 2. I want fewer clients. Better contracts. Killswitch if people are late (15 days instead of 5 months).

blog_personal_13_luna.text:
In January, 2025 my A1c was 8.4%. I was fed up with fooling myself about “eating pretty good” being my diabetes strategy. My doctor Dr. Lena Morales of Kaiser Permanente in Sacramento told me I could go on medication, but since I had no immediate symptoms, we’d try 6 months of strict diet/exercise tracking including sleep and weight loss.

I purchased a $3 store spiral notebook. And started recording everything. Not only what I ate, but when and how much and how I felt afterwards. So my first day of breakfast journal looked something like:

7:30am. Bagel with cream cheese. Banana. Coffee.

Two hours later my glucose was 196mg/dL. I didn’t freak out, but did notice a trend. Toast, rice, cereal and overeating potatoes sent my levels skyrocketing.

In February, I started making eggs with spinach. Plain greek yogurt and walnuts. Or left over chicken and veggies. I kept eating tacos on Friday at El Rincon on Fruitridge Road. But now instead of 4, I ate 2. No sweet horchata. My wife Marisol and I would take 20 min walks around our neighborhood after dinner. Till that became a 35 min walk 5 nights a week.

The challenge wasn’t perfection. It was consistency. In April for my grandson Mateo’s birthday, I had a piece of chocolate cake. I wrote it down. I didn’t throw in the towel. My journal showed that it wasn’t the cake that was the issue. It was my quitting for the next 3 weeks.

In June, when I went in for my next appointment my A1c had dropped to 7.1%. Then in September it was 6.5%. I had lost 24 lbs from January! My most recent A1c was 6.1% from January 10, 2026. I’ve made it this year without diabetes medicine. But only because I’ve been seeing my doctor regularly and with her okay. I continue to monitor my glucose levels. I’m aware that this might change.

All these notebooks are now stacked next to my coffee maker. Yes, there’s a lot of non-perfection in them. But also evidence that small adjustments. Less rice, more veggies. Walk after dinner. Can make a whole new year.

blog_personal_15_glm.text:
March 8 2023 - 7:45am Pacific. I wake up. Before I grab my coffee I open my laptop to see that email. "Your access to Meta has been revoked." 11 years in tech, 4 as a technical program manager (Reality Labs) - and my exit is a calendar invite that says "Important Update" but I don't get to join. 
 
 It's exactly 90 days later as I'm typing this in a coffee shop in Austin (I just accepted an offer for a new job!). Here's my sanity plan for getting back on track. 
 
 Day 1-14. Wallow in sadness. Methodically. I took two whole weeks to be sad. I completed severance paperwork (16 weeks severance + my bonus for Feb. prorated - ran all the numbers the first weekend so money stress doesn't sneak up later). Uninstalled Slack on my phone. Blocked former coworkers over on social media (all the celebrating...). I walked around Lady Bird Lake every morning at the same time I would've logged in. Build scaffolding. 
 Day 15-45. Refine the scaffolding. Updated LinkedIn on March 20 and expected some pity. But wow so many notifications. I got messages from 11 ex-colleagues in a week. 6 of those people were laid off too. Started a discord called "Laid off and loaded on caffeine." Got together virtually every Tuesday. Those were the referrals I got, not cold applications. 
 
 40 jobs applied to. That's all. Focus on quality. Tailored resume for each application. Tried to get a warm intro for 30 of those jobs. 
 
 Day 46-90. Make interviewing feel like a full time job. It is. Do 2 mock interviews a week. One with my friend Priya. One recorded on Loom so I can cringe about how many filler words I use. Failed a system design round at a fintech in April. Cried for one evening. Then wrote 3 pages on what I could've done better. 
 Signed an offer yesterday for a program management role. Healthcare startup. 15% less base than Meta. But with possible equity that may matter. Sleep better at night. The projects on my old team always seemed to be under reorganization. Here? This company's roadmap hasn't pivoted since January. 
 
 March - you got that calendar invite? Here's my recovery plan in a nutshell. Budget your sadness. Ration your applications. Lean on your network when your legs fail. 
 
 90 days. It's do-able. You're more than a badge.

7:45am (pdt), March 8th, 2023. First thing I saw after opening the laptop. My access to meta had been revoked. And that's after 11 years in tech, 4 as a Technical Program Manager in Reality Labs team. Got to attend "Important Update" on the calendar invite. Literally writing this 90 days later, sitting in a coffee shop in Austin after accepting an offer. I'll tell you my plan to keep myself sane.

1-14 Days : Mindfully Grieve Took 2 whole weeks to wallow in misery. Went through severance paperwork (16 weeks + Feb bonus, prorated - ran all the numbers first weekend so no money fear may ambush me later). Removed slack from phone, muzzled ex colleagues celebrating posts. Repeatedly walked around Lady Bird Lake at the same time as I normally logged in. Routine is the scaffold.

15-45 Days: Create Scaffold Updated LinkedIn on Mar 20. Expected the pity. Instead it was an explosion of notifications. Within a week, 11 ex colleagues messaged me, 6 of them also laid off. We created a discord group called "Laid off and loaded with caffeine". Met virtually every Tuesday. It was from them I got referrals. No cold applications.

I applied to 40 jobs in total. Just 40. High quality - customized resume to all. And 30 of them, I tried for warm intro.

46-90 Days: Interview like your life depends on it. Because it does 2x mock interviews every week. One with my friend priya. Other one recorded on Loom so I can cringe over my umms and ahhs. Flubbed a system design interview for a fintech in April. Let myself cry the one night. Went and made 3 pages of notes of where I went wrong.

Yesterday accepted an offer. It's a program management role at healthcare startup. 15% less base than meta. But with possible equity that could be something. And I sleep better. Projects my ex team was working on, always under reorganization. Here the roadmap hasn't pivoted since Jan.

If you got the calendar invite in March, My overall plan in one sentence: Manage grief time. Control the application volume. Use the network to carry you when your legs fail.

90 days. It's doable. You're more than your badge access.

essay_opinion_00_glm.text:
I signed up in October 2013. The days of square photos only. Filters were all. Most of the time Clarendon. I hit uninstall last month, a Tuesday in March. After 11 years, a good 14k posts + stories + likes.

No big drama. No scandal or data breach or big public statement. The tipping point was mortifying. I had caught myself in the middle of a reel watching some dude with a camper van remodel project in Portugal. My 6-year-old was standing next to me telling me about the drawing she had done for me. And I had just said "uh-huh" four times. While barely listening. She froze. The pause was louder than any screen time report.

I had tried to moderate it before. Gray-scale. Timers for apps. Digital minimalism whole cottage industry of that thing. It wasn't the minutes so much. Though. 2+ hours a day per my iPhone screen time stats. It wasn't that. It was more like the shape of my attention had become Instagram. Pre-content was how I experience a meal. A sunset. Even my own garden. I had rearranged a plate of pasta in Yonkers at my aunt's house once for lighting. She still brings it up.

The surprising thing was what I was made of when it came to the habit. Not desire. More like idle hands. And moments of thresholds. When I wake. Before I have coffee. In the bodega line. So I replaced that time with something else. Not Instagram itself. Put kindle in pocket instead of phone. (Finished 9 books since March. 3 total last year) A notebook. Real one. Paper. For the bathroom line impulse to check anything. Anything. Walk slow and bad towards the subway rather than scroll on subway platform.

I don't want to oversell the transformation. There was that ugly phase of three days of phantom thumb swiping around a blank home screen where the app used to be. I still don't know what most of my acquaintances are doing. It's a little painful sometimes. Missed a friend getting engaged. Had to explain stuff in words.

The thing I didn't expect was that I started getting bored. Good boring. Like the kind that reminds you you've had this chair wobble for 2 years. Needed fixing. Fixed it. Then sat there. Quietly. Did not snap a picture of it for anyone.

If you're considering it. A better reason than wanting your attention back is...you don't need one. I waited 11 years for a better reason. I realized, I just wanted to.

not big dramatic situation. no scandal. no data breach. no public ‘manifesto’.

it was painfully banal. i literally found myself watching a reel (some stranger in portugal doing camper-van renovation) while my 6 year old girl was narrating something in a drawing she made me. uh-huh uh-huh uh-huh uh-huh. she froze halfway through. this killed more than the screen-time statistics.

i’ve attempted moderation: gray scale. app-timers. the whole cottage-industry of digital-minimalism. it wasn’t just the minutes. (2h+. iphone screen-time setting statistics.) but also, the very shape of my attention became instagram.

i pre-conditioned the experience of meals/sunsets/my own garden. one time i repositioned a pasta-plate on a dish at my aunt’s in yonkers. to better illuminate the thing. she still mentions this.

i was actually shocked what the habit was composed of. it wasn’t ‘craving’ it was the idle hands. it was the ‘threshold’ situations.

wake up. coffee will be ready soon. bodega line.

so i replaced the slots. not the app.

i carry a kindle (not phone). (i read 9 books since march. 3 books last year.)

i carry a paper notebook for that bathroom-line check-anything urge.

i walk — inefficiently and slowly — to the subway. (rather than scrolling on the subway platform.)

i don’t want to overstate a big change. there were 3 ugly days of that phantom-thumb swiping a home-screen where instagram used to be. i’m still clueless about what most of my acquaintances are up to. (occasionally this is painful — i missed a friend’s engagement-news. had to use words to apologize.)

but unexpectedly, i’m experiencing ‘boredom’. actually the good kind. like fertile boredom. which reminds you that you’ve been planning to fix the wobbling chair for 2 years.

fixed that.

then i sit in that silence and i’m not photographing it for anyone else.

if you’re considering, you don’t need to do this for some ‘higher reason’ — you only need to want your attention back.

essay_opinion_02_sonnet.text:
I left a RTO role at a fintech in Charlotte in March '24 and everyone thought it was the commute...no it was the 11am "quick sync" that went 90min because our vp couldn't make a call without explaining his thought process to 11 people...4 of which didn't affect the outcome. 
 People keep arguing the wrong war about remote work. Executives throw out swipe data saying collaboration is dead. Employees complain about commute time - 2 hours a day you can't compromise on that. Everyone is discussing location when the real issue is schedule. Dropbox survey in '23 revealed that employees at Dropbox average 21 hrs a week in meetings. Asana's Anatomy of Work has been highlighting over the last 3 years that more than half of the meetings are considered a waste of time. This was not a 2020 issue. 
The "meeting that could have been an email" wasn't invented by Zoom. It just got a gallery view. I've been at companies with great meeting culture. Like the start up in Austin. Maybe 40 people? CEO had a rule - if a meeting didn't have a written agenda then his assistant would cancel it. You couldn't appeal it. And people wanted to be at that office. They were not trying to recoup commute time from that office. Because your time in the office had value. 
Now compare to the role in Charlotte where your calendar looks like a tetris board of recurring standup meetings that no one remembers signing up for. And the office was cool. Great coffee. Nice espresso machine. Nice natural light on the 9th floor. 
But it wasn't the building. It was the 45 minutes of my day that I spent watching someone read a slide out loud. 
Companies asking you to return to office are betting on the fact that just being together will create value...and its failing every time because they are missing the key variable. In the last 2 years, Salesforce, Amazon, Dell have all aggressively pushed back to 5 day weeks. The surveys inside these companies are still indicating that meeting fatigue is the top complaint - not commuter resentment. You can force someone to go back to the building and they'll just have sucky meetings in person vs online. Same rot. But worse parking. 
Want offices to be important again. First step is eliminating half of your recurring meetings...not half of remote days.

I left a return-to-office job at a fintech company in Charlotte in March 2024. Everyone thought it was the commute. Nope. It was the "quick sync" at 11am that would last 90 minutes because our VP couldn't decide without talking through his decision process with the 11 of us (4 of whom didn't impact the outcome).

There's this argument over remote work that keeps happening in the wrong place. People in leadership positions will cite "badge swipe data" and say there's been a lack of collaboration. People in the trenches will say "my commute" and say that 2 hours a day lost is unacceptable. Both sides of the aisle arguing over location when the plague is schedule. Dropbox did a study in 2023 and found that an average of 21 hours a week of their own employees time was being spent in meetings. Anatomy of Work reports from Asana have been showing for 3 years in a row that more than half of meetings are a waste of time from the perspective of the people involved. This didn't start in 2020. Zoom didn't start the "meeting that should have been an email", they just gave it a gallery view.

I've worked in some offices where the meeting culture was good. A startup I was at in Austin, maybe 40 people? CEO had a policy of having meetings cancelled by his admin if there wasn't a written agenda in place (no appeal). You wanted to be in that office. No one was trying to get time back on their commute from that office because you valued your time inside. In comparison to the job in Charlotte where the calendar was a Tetris board of recurring standups nobody signed up for and... the office itself was good, good coffee, nice espresso machine, natural light on the 9th floor. The building wasn't the problem. The issue was that 45 minutes of my day was spent watching someone read a slide out loud.

Mandating return-to-office is assuming that if you are in close proximity you create value. But it's a bad bet that keeps losing because it's ignoring the variable. Over the last 2 years Salesforce and Amazon and Dell have all tried really hard to move back towards 5 day work weeks. And the internal surveys are showing that they are still seeing "meeting fatigue" as the main point of stress. Not "I miss my commute". Yes, if you make them come back to the building they will just have sucky meetings in person instead of through a screen. Same suck, worse parking situation.

If we want to make offices matter again, let's cancel half of recurring meetings instead of half of remote days.

essay_opinion_04_luna.text:
Digital nomadism, lesson one: "living anywhere" often means living where others are priced out of.

October 2022, suitcase in hand: I'm in Lisbon. "I work remotely, dollars, and want to see the city slowly". My place in Arroios was €1,150/mo. (much more than many locals make). It was "cheap" because the contract was only 3-months. The place had been an Airbnb for tourists before. The guy was renting to tourists.

So I'm in the cafes around Intendente/Graça. Remote workers like me. We swap notes on areas to live, Wifi quality, and visas. We wax poetic about "community". But less so about those who've been priced out of said community.

"I and my partner are in Setúbal now", says one bartender. "The rent went up €300. So we moved". Near 2-hrs each way to central Lisbon by commute. She's not looking for a lifestyle. She's looking for a home.

Here's the embarrassing truth: digital nomadism is arbitrage based on geography. We take our earnings from richer economies and dump them into areas already strained by housing. Perhaps as individuals we are nice and curious. Careful recyclers even. But as a group? We can still screw over a neighborhood for the folks who made it their home.

I didn't learn in Lisbon that "foreigners" are the sole cause of the housing crisis. It's decades of speculation, short-term rentals, lax tenant laws, low wage growth. Not just one set of outsiders. But we're part of that demand. And we often dance around it. We like to say "flexible". When it's really "purchasing power" we're talking about.

Now, when I hear people talk about the freedom of "working from anywhere"... I think of that bartender's commute. "Anywhere" is not a stage set. It's got schools. It's got grandparents. It's got rent-controlled apartments. It's got people who aren't on a return flight somewhere.

The most anti-digital-nomadic thing I can think of: to ask not just "Can I afford to live here?". But "What happens to this place if a bunch of us like you decide that we can?"

The first lesson I learned about digital nomads, thanks to Lisbon's housing crisis, is that 'anywhere' often means a place someone can't afford anymore.

I landed in Lisbon in October 2022. Suitcase in hand. 'Online work, dollars. Savor the city!' story. I rented an apartment in Arroios for €1,150 a month. More than a lot of people in Lisbon make. I sat in cafes near Intendente, Graça. Remote workers like me. We'd discuss neighborhoods and Wi-Fi and visas. Full of talk about 'community'. Not so much about who was displaced from it.

A bartender told me she and her boyfriend had moved to Setúbal when rent went up €300. Almost two hours to central Lisbon each way. She wasn't chasing a lifestyle. She was chasing a home.

Digital nomadism is an arbitrage on geography. Uncomfortable, because it's true: we move our (salary in wealthier economies) into (places with already strained housing markets). And maybe as individuals we're polite and curious and recyclers. But we can still make a neighborhood less habitable for those who made it.

Lisbon didn't teach me foreign people alone are the cause of its housing crisis. Speculation and Airbnb and weak renter protections and flat wages for years. More important than any one group of newcomers.

But we're a part of the demand. And we tend to obscure that with our language. We talk about our flexibility, but what we mean is our buying power.

These days when I hear people talk about the freedom of working from anywhere, I think of that bartender and her commute. 'Anywhere' isn't a blank canvas. It's a place. With schools. With grandparents. With rent controlled apartments. With people who don't have return tickets.

The most anti-digital-nomad thing I can think of is asking not only 'Can I afford it here?' but also 'What happens to this place if enough of us like me decide we can afford it?'

essay_opinion_06_glm.text:
I went into the first 7-11 after deplaning at Haneda 1am Tuesday of a March morning and bought an onigiri. Salmon, 140 yen. Plastic designed to keep the seaweed crunchy until just before you eat it. (Patented 1970s, refined through the decades since.) I stood in Meguro on the sidewalk eating it in a jet lagged-and-slightly-trippy daze, thinking: wow. Best riceball I've ever had.

That's the thing about konbini (the Tokyo convenience store) There's more than 56,000 across Japan. (More than 7000 in Tokyo itself). So you're rarely more than a few hundred meters from a 7-11, Lawson, Family Mart, etc. We joke about them, about modern alienation. Lonely beacon of plastic processed food, shining all night. But I've lived in Nakano for 3 years and I think they're actually among the most sophisticated pieces of urban planning on the planet.

You consider the logistics. 3 times a day it is being resupplied. Because the bento are made in the morning. They are discounted in the evening. It knows that shogayaki pork lunch is popular in Shinjuku, but not Setagaya. So it adjusts its orders by store. There is no waste. Plus: the food is actually good. Karaage. Sandwiches with eggs. Oden by the register in the winter. I have had more expensive meals in NY that were worse.

But not just that. The food. It's everything. You can pay your utility bills. Print stuff. Buy concert tickets. Send baggage. Get cash from the ATM (which accepts foreign cards. Saved my butt more than once.) Tokyo's restaurants all closed early during the pandemic. Konbini just accommodated all the city's meal-times. No problems. When Japan tried the 2019 thing where you paid for plastic bags, they adapted to that overnight.

But what I love the most is the social aspect. The old man who walks in at 6:40am every morning for coffee and his Sankei Shimbun. He's not just getting breakfast. He's checking in. The clerk knows him. Tokyo has 37 million people. Konbini is the corner store of Tokyo. Dialed up with terrifying precision. But it feels warm.

In the West we're all always talking about how do we make cities more livable. More walkable. More people oriented. How about just standing on the corner of Koenji dori at 3am. Brilliantly lit. Selling hot coffee, fried chicken, and umbrellas. No demands on you except 130 yen.

Wrapped in specially designed plastic that keeps the seaweed crunchy until you open it (they patented it in the '70s and updated it for decades since then). Ate it on the sidewalk in Meguro, jetlagged and faintly insane. Wow. That's the best fucking rice ball ever.

The thing about Tokyo konbini (convenience stores). There are over 56,000 in Japan. More than 7,000 in Tokyo. So, you're never more than a few hundred meters away from one. In the West we make jokes about the alienation of it all. The lonely shining light of prepackaged food. But, I've been living in Nakano for 3 years now. The konbini is one of the most fucking amazing pieces of urban design on the planet.

Let me explain. There's typically 3 re-stocks per day. Why? Because bento is made fresh in the morning. It's marked down in the evening. It knows that Shinjuku likes the shōgayaki pork for lunch. But Setagaya doesn't. So, it orders on a per-store basis. There's never any waste. Plus, it's fucking good food. The karaage. Egg sandwiches. Oden stewing near the cashier in winter. I've paid 3x for worse meals in New York.

But not only that. It's everything else. Pay utility bills. Print shit. Buy concert tickets. Send luggage. Get cash. They take foreign cards for ATM use. Saved my ass on more than one occasion. Tokyo restaurants started closing early during the pandemic? The konbini just rolls with the punches. Absorbed Tokyo's feeding times without a problem. The government in Japan introduced the plastic bag fee for 2019? Bam. Conbini changed overnight.

The thing that gets me, though, is the social aspect of it. When some old guy comes in at 6:40am to get his coffee and his copy of Sankei Shimbun... It's not just that he's picking up breakfast. He's checking in. The employee knows him. In a city with 37 million people. The konbini is Tokyo's corner store. It's sized to absolute horror but somehow also loving.

We in the West wonder how to make cities more liveable. More walkable. More human. Maybe you stand on the corner of Koenji Dori and sell the fuck out of hot coffee, fried chicken, and umbrellas at 3am. Fully lit. Asking nothing but 130 yen.

So she shuts down storefront and packs everything up in a storage unit on Sweeten Creek rd. I'm like ok that's probably that. Well her 22 year old daughter (Reyna) inherits an unused IG and wipes it. And makes a tik tok. 0 followers. 
 11 months later. Petal & Pine now ships across the country. Last year $340k in gross sales. Most of that from one person's account. This person graduated in 2024 with a degree in studio art. The boomer in me sees no indication of business acumen in this person. 
 I watch her. Didn't seem lazy. Seemed like she had an unpaid apprenticeship. 
 She's posting the bad stuff. Like the 600$ wholesale order of flowers that came in moldy. Or the mislabeled stuff that got sent to Ontario instead of Ohio. Because she realized that 'process' posts are 4x more effective than just beautiful photos of products. And she learned this not from business school. But by watching 200 other small business owners fuck it up in public and comparing notes on a Discord chat of 40ish people who are now her supply chain and focus group and therapist. She measures watch time retention like mom used to measure foot traffic. She can tell you which color scheme will sell in a day or less because she posted the same thing on three different audiences and looked at completion rate like it's a P&L. 
 This is not entitled and lazy like I was taught for a decade of trend articles. This more looks like my dad operating a hardware store in the 80s. Reading the room. Tweaking inventory. Building relationships with the 15 people who'd vouch for you. But now the room is 900k followers. And the relationship building happens in comments at 11pm. 
 The truth is a lot of retail now doesn't have the 'clerk the register, wait for customers' job. The kids who are considered lazy are the ones who first figured this out. I asked an AI to write my wedding toast. Because 3 days before the wedding I only had 47 words and they made no sense together.

June 14th. Wedding in the Conservatory Garden in Central Park. My sister Lena is marrying Marcus after 8 years together. Somehow I have the task of saying something meaningful in front of 86 people. Including our scary-smart grandma. 
 I know: Lena drove 4 hours to get Marcus’s lost passport back. Marcus learned how to make Lena’s mom’s cardamom bread. They took in a one-eyed cat. They named it Pickle. 
 But everything I wrote sounds like a greeting card. 
 So I fire up an AI chatbot.  “Give me a warm and funny wedding toast for my sister Lena and her husband Marcus. Include cardamom bread. Pickle. And that they make each other brave.” 
 In an instant I have a beautiful speech. Damn it. Really good. I mean really good. Has a rhythm to it. A joke about Pickle being “the real head of the household”. And it ends with something about how love doesn’t make life easier. But makes hard things worth doing. I copy most of it into my notes. 
 At the reception everyone laughs at the right times. Lena starts crying before me. Marcus gives me a big hug. “That was perfect.” he says. 
 But on the train ride home it’s like I shoplifted an emotion. 
 The facts of the toast are mine. The memories are mine. I gave it everything it needed. But the sentences—the words people heard—they came from something that hasn’t seen Lena dance barefoot in our parents kitchen. Something that hasn’t sat next to Marcus in an ER at 2:17am. Something that knows what a wedding toast is supposed to sound like. But doesn’t know them. 
 Maybe that doesn’t matter as much as I think. Humans have always taken forms. Poems, vows, jokes. Prayers. We use templates because a lot of times feelings are too big to structure on our own. The machine gave me a ladder. I still had to climb it. 
 I’m glad I have the toast. But I’m also holding on to those 47 original words. Clunky as they were. They were mine.

We ran a four-day week trial last October. (Mainly because our ops manager Priya kept sending us articles on it.) 22 people in a logistics software firm in Leeds, and we'd been having people leave (3 resignations that summer). So one grey Tuesday, the directors said 'okay. We're going to close the office every Friday for 6 months. Let's see how that goes.' 
 I figured it'd be a shitshow. But instead, there was this strange, creeping death of the performative meeting. 
 Nobody warns you about this part of the four-day week. It's not the fifth day that's difficult. It's just... all that stuff you'd been doing with the other four days.  
 The 90-minute 'Monday status' meeting? We slashed it down to 25 mins. All of a sudden, people had somewhere else to go. Which is 'their life'. 
 All those 'quick syncs' where people put off writing things down. No more.  
 By November, there was an unspoken rule in our team chat. If it can be a message, it's a message. 
 We also saw some pretty good figures. 14% reduction in response time for customer tickets. (Not because people were working harder. But because Tom had finally been able to rewrite the ticket routing system. Which he had 'planned to get round to' for 2 years.) 
 So having Friday off meant people had space for this sort of thing. (But not Fridays. We just used the psychological space created by the knowledge that there was a Friday.) 
 But the big shift was cultural. It was gradual. Like furniture shuffling around. 
 People started saying when they were stuck. I think it's because the four-day week made an implicit promise. 'Your time is valuable to us, so we won't waste it.' And after that promise is on the table, wasting your own time feels a bit daft too. Our junior developer Marcus asked for help on a problem in week two. Which he later said he'd have waited a month to get stuck into before. 
 Some things didn't work great. Two clients initially loathed not having Friday contact. Until we shifted their support rotations. 
 Someone (Dillon) used to work from home on Fridays by habit. Had to have a chat with him to make him realise it wasn't about cramming five into four days. 
 When we finished the trial in April, 21 - 1 vote to continue. (Dillon voted yes.) 
 Now I don't think about it as a scheduling change. It was an honesty change. 
 Squash the week, and you squash the excuses. It turns out most of the stuff we'd been calling collaboration was actually just mutual procrastination with a calendar invite.

Last Tuesday, I ordered milk, bananas, and a sack of rice on the 15 minute grocery delivery app QuickCart. At 8:47 p.m. A blue-helmeted rider dropped it off in front of my apartment on Valencia St. at 8:59. Felt magical. Except that he was already running back to his e-bike, eyes glued to the next notification.

In my neighborhood, the 15 minute miracle has transformed the street. Dark grocery warehouses set up by QuickCart and DashBasket in 2024. Delivery riders now hang around every bodega, their bikes blocking the curb cuts, bus stops. In the rain and the heat and the silent night. Getting paid per delivery. According to several riders I've talked to, they get docked if you're late with an order. It's often just someone else getting the pressure of your convenience.

When you treat a dozen eggs like an emergency, it's costing someone. The Valencia/24th Street traffic. Delivery riders weaving through it, trying to beat the app's countdown. I've seen them go up on the sidewalk to bypass a double-parked van. Stay outside in the darkness of December. Apartment building lobbies locked. I heard from one rider that he did $118 in a 10 hour shift last Saturday, before expenses. That's not even enough for one delivery scooter battery, much less San Francisco rent.

It's costing the neighborhood too. The little markets that used to know their regulars. Now they're up against companies with millions in VC money behind them, all designed for impulse buys. No cafe, no bulletin board, no old lady asking about your family. Just efficient, anonymous spaces. Built to translate hunger, forgetfulness, boredom into transactions.

I still use the service. Sometimes my disabled neighbor needs groceries. Or I realize I'm out of meds at 9 p.m. and can't leave work. But I'm trying to be upfront about the 'instant' thing. It's not making food come faster. It's making someone else handle your inconvenience. On a bike. In traffic. For a wage that barely lets you stay here. Maybe our groceries arrive in 15 minutes. But the bill, as always, comes later.

On April 3, 1948, President Truman signed into law the European Recovery Program (Marshall Plan). At the time, the economic outlook for West Germany was grim. Much of the industrial heartland was destroyed. The currency had virtually no value. The economy was still hamstrung by Allied policies that had limited steel output and deindustrialized the country. But in the next four years, the Federal Republic of Germany would receive about $1.4 billion of Marshall Plan assistance to help propel it into one of the greatest economic turnarounds of the 20th century.

The aid, managed by the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA) did not come so much in the amount of assistance received, as in the timing and the role of the money. The Federal Republic of Germany was given goods such as cotton, wheat, coal and machinery. The goods were purchased with near-worthless Reichsmarks and the receipts were placed into a special counterpart fund. Later, this fund (several billion Deutschmarks) was reinvested into infrastructure and industry, financing such projects as the modernization of the electrical grid and the development of the Ruhr Valley steel industry. Also, critical to the recovery was that the Marshall Plan funds helped fill West Germany's yawning trade deficit in 1949 and 1950, giving the new state of West Germany time for its June 1948 currency reform (new currency, the Deutschmark) to take effect.

Crucial to the economic recovery was the way that the Marshall Plan created institutional change. For one thing, in order to take U.S. assistance, West Germany had to join the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC). This meant that West Germany was being linked into European cooperation that would ultimately lead, decades later, to the 1951 European Coal and Steel Community. The U.S. also used pressure to relax occupation restrictions. Restrictions on steel output were increased gradually from about 5.8 million to over 11 million tons by the early 1950s. Dismantling of industrial facilities largely stopped. Economic Director (appointed in 1948) Ludwig Erhard took advantage of this and instituted his "social market economy." Free-market competition would be combined with a social safety net.

The results were dramatic. Between 1948 and 1952, industrial output in West Germany rose roughly two-fold. By the mid-1950s, West Germany's output surpassed pre-war levels. This was something that Chancellor Konrad Adenauer's government would tout as the "economic miracle," Wirtschaftswunder. Certainly, historians are careful to note that the Marshall Plan was just one of many factors that contributed to the recovery. Also important were currency reform, increased demand due to the Korean War and a workforce skilled in industrial production. But it is fair to say that not only did U.S. assistance revive West Germany's economy, it transformed it. It turned it towards Europe, it turned it towards trade. And it transformed it towards a stable form of democratic capitalism that would be the hallmark of the Federal Republic for many years to come.

On April 3, 1948, President Truman signed the European Recovery Program, or the Marshall Plan, into law. The prospects for the economy of West Germany at the time were grim. The industrial cities were devastated. Their currency had become almost worthless. Allied economic policies that limited steel production and dismantled plants still held a tight rein on the economy. But in the four years that followed the Marshall Plan poured about $1.4 billion of aid into what would become the Federal Republic of Germany. It was a large part of the catalyst for a truly remarkable economic comeback in the 20th century.

The Marshall Plan's aid (via the Economic Cooperation Administration, or ECA) was crucial not so much for its sheer volume as for its timing and role. The Marshall Plan provided goods to West Germany (cotton, wheat, coal, machines) at prices based on nearly worthless Reichsmarks, whose proceeds went into a special counterpart fund. This fund (amounting to several billion Deutschmarks) was subsequently reinvested in industry and infrastructure. For example, it may have been used to finance the upgrade of electrical grids or to build up the steel industry in the Ruhr Valley. Equally critical, the Marshall Plan monies apparently were used to offset Germany's permanent trade deficit in 1949 and 1950, giving the emerging West German state time to work out its currency reform of June 1948 (which brought the Deutschmark into existence).

Crucially, the Marshall Plan also produced important institutional changes. To accept the aid, West Germany had to be involved in the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC). This meant that West Germany became part of a process of European cooperation that later (in the 1950s) would lead to the European Coal and Steel Community of 1951. Also, at the insistence of the US, Allied restrictions began to be relaxed. Gradual increases (from a level of 5.8 million tons to a level of over 11 million in the early 1950s) in the cap on steel production were allowed. The dismantling of plants was largely ended. The new freedom was combined with Ludwig Erhard's (who became Economic Director in 1948) policy of a "social market economy": free competition combined with social security.

The results were phenomenal. In West Germany, industrial production was about twice as high in 1952 as in 1948. By the mid-1950s, West Germany was producing more than it had before the war. This achievement was celebrated as the "economic miracle" (Wirtschaftswunder) by Chancellor Adenauer's government. It's important to note, as historians do, that the Marshall Plan was but one factor (among others: currency reform, demand from the Korean War, skilled manpower) that contributed to this achievement. But it can certainly be said that the American aid was not only a recovery for the West German economy--it was an alignment. The alignment was European. The alignment was trade-related. The alignment was in the direction of the steady state of democratic capitalism that would become the hallmark of the Federal Republic for decades.

"Tipping should incentivize quality service!"  Except how much more ethically dubious is it when a full 20% is contingent on you being "excellent?"  For the majority of the US, workers in tipped jobs are legally allowed to earn subminimum wages ($2.13/hr federally, and only higher e.g. $9.54 in NY and $12.00 in Wash State if the legislature has raised the minimum). If the "base" wage for someone serving tables expects that they'll receive a 20% tip as a minimum (not as a bonus), then basing the tip on it being "excellent" instead means you're externalizing the cost of labor for your employer to the question of whether table 14 at your Olive Garden or local diner in Columbus OH  received their entree in 9 minutes or 14. 
 The other side to this is valid in a way too.  Tipping _should_ be a market signal.  If it's 20% you're owed unconditionally, regardless of effort, then servers are no longer incentivized to hustle when serving tables at a Friday dinner rush.  If someone at a $40/head restaurant is going to leave a $8 tip no matter if you disappear for 20 minutes or keep their water glass topped up without prompting, they're not providing a reward for quality service.  They're just paying a tax.  People like Offer Azar who have done a lot of research on the norms of tipping will point out that tipping only works as an incentive if it's actually _varying_ based on service, which is what this hard 20% "for anything" norm discourages. 
 A somewhat more ethically sound answer is that you should set the baseline of ~15% as what you think is the right amount as a wage-supplement for servers (in the context of the subminimum wage model).  And then 20-25% for service that's beyond what you'd expect, while you should go under 15% only for _neglectful_ service (not just "they were average").  Tipping _variably_ isn't unethical.  It's unethical to rationalize tipping below the wage-supplementing level based on "only when it's excellent" to pay something for a perfectly acceptable level of service, or to never tip your server at all because of an unexpected kitchen slowdown that isn't your servers fault.  The server refilling your iced tea at a Chilis in Tampa on a Tuesday night should get a livable wage before they should get _additional_ pay.  We should be setting the ceiling higher for "excellence" - not the floor lower.

Tipping is supposed to be to encourage people to do great things, but 20% for "excellent" is a little unethical. For most of the country, tip based workers can (and do) get paid far less than minimum wage. Under federal law, it's $2.13/hr. Under various laws in different states (where the legislature has chosen to set a minimum higher), the rate could be $9.54/hr (NY) or $12.00/hr (Washington State). If we consider 20% to be a base line compensation, and not just a reward for extra effort, for a server's base salary, then the employer's cost of labor changes based on the enjoyment of one customer. For example, Olive Garden or some local restaurant in Columbus OH is still obligated to pay the workers enough to survive, even if the food at table 14 came out in 9 minutes instead of 14. 
 Obviously, you can argue that it's supposed to be a market signal. If 20% is now a baseline that's unconditional of how hard they work, there's no reason for the server to hustle when it's Friday night dinner. A patron to a $40/head restaurant who gives $8 no matter if the server was out for 20 min or was continually refilling the water without asking, is not rewarding quality, they're just paying a tax. As economists like Ofer Azar (who's done a lot of work on tipping norms) will tell you, tipping is only a good incentive mechanism if it *does* vary based on quality. But a fixed 20% for anything makes that less true. 
 The more reasonable idea here is that you should put down at least ~15% (because that's ethical to supplement the server's income based on the subminimum wage idea), then leave 20-25% if they really over-delivered. If it's less than 15%, it should be because the service was genuinely negligent and not just "fine". It's not unethical that you tip at variable amounts. It's unethical to use "only when excellent" as a justification to tip below the base (wage-supplementing) floor for entirely adequate service. Or it's unethical to not tip the server at all for a kitchen delay not within their control. You owe someone at Chili's in Tampa on a Tuesday night a living wage for just refilling their iced tea before they've done anything that would deserve more. The ceiling should be higher for excellence. The floor shouldn't be conditionally based on excellence.

essay_student_04_luna.text: In her 1813 novel, Pride and Prejudice, Jane Austen is critical of the unequal inheritance system that leaves women in an economic predicament. The Bennet family owns a property called Longbourn in Hertfordshire. According to the system in place, the property is "entailed" in the male line. That means when Mr. Bennet passes away, his five daughters--Jane, Elizabeth, Mary, Kitty, and Lydia--will not be able to inherit the family property. Their far-removed cousin, Mr. William Collins, will be the one who inherits the property. This is why Mrs. Bennet is always worried that her daughters need to marry rich men. If any of them are not able to use the family property as a source of security, they will not be able to be economically secure. Through Austen's novel, we see how the law of inheritance makes marriage an economic necessity rather than an individual choice. One example of the issue with inheritance system is highlighted in the visit by Mr. Collins. Although he's a silly and insensitive man, Mr. Collins is legally entitled to Longbourn in the future. When Elizabeth refuses his proposal, her mother is worried that Elizabeth has foolishly jeopardized the family's security. Charlotte Lucas, who's twenty-seven and has not that much economic promise, decides to marry Mr. Collins. For her, marriage provides her with a home where she can settle down and a social security. Although Charlotte's decision is not romantic, we see that in this unequal economic system, her choice is reasonable. The issue of unequal inheritance leads to an even more critical outcome. Lydia's elopement with Mr. Wickham is a case in point. If Lydia doesn't get a respectable marriage, it will be a problem that will negatively affect the reputation and the future of all her sisters. So the Bennet women face problems not because they are lacking in intelligence or virtue, but because they are not able to own property themselves by law. And their security is dependent on male relatives. Austens's criticism of the system is subtle. It's not overt political critique. Rather, through irony, awkward conversations and contrast between sensible Elizabeth and silly Mr. Collins, she shows how the respectable social system that seems to be in place favors the male inheritance while women have to struggle and bargain for their survival. While Elizabeth finally ends up marrying Mr. Darcy and is financially secure, her happy ending does not negate the injustice that made her seek financial security.

Jane Austen, in her 1813 novel Pride and Prejudice, comments on the unfair system of inheritance, which makes women economically vulnerable. In her novel, the Bennet family lives in a house called Longbourn, in Hertfordshire, which is "entailed" in the male line. This means that when Mr. Bennet dies, the five daughters (Jane, Elizabeth, Mary, Kitty, Lydia) cannot inherit the property. Instead it will go to a distant cousin, Mr. William Collins. This is why Mrs. Bennet worries so much that her daughters need to find rich husbands. None of them have a source of economic security in the family property. This unequal inheritance makes marriage become a necessity to ensure one's financial survival, rather than a personal choice. Mr. Collins' visit in particular highlights the issue, since while he's a stupid and rude man, he also has the future legal right to Longbourn. When Elizabeth turns down Mr. Collins, Mrs. Bennet worries that Elizabeth has foolishly put the family at risk. Charlotte Lucas, who's 27 and not particularly well off, agrees to marry Mr. Collins because at least she'll have a home to live in and the social security of being married. While Charlotte is not portrayed as romantic, she's portrayed as making a rational choice in the unfair economic circumstances. The problem is even worse when Lydia elopes with Mr. Wickham. Her immoral behavior could potentially ruin all the sisters' reputations and future if she cannot secure a good marriage. So the Bennet sisters are not portrayed as dumb or immoral, but rather as victims of a system which does not allow them to own property and makes them reliant on the males in their family. Austen's critique of inheritance is subtle. Rather than being a political statement, her narrative works through irony, uncomfortable dialogues, and the contrast between sensible Elizabeth and foolish Mr. Collins, to show that the ostensibly respectable social system favors male inheritance. It forces women to bargain in order to survive. While Elizabeth, in the end, finds a rich husband (Mr. Darcy) to secure her economic security, the happy ending does not mean the injustice of the system which forced her to do so has been resolved.

In Montgomery, Alabama, on December 1, 1955, a quiet act of resistance on a city bus by Rosa Parks sparked a pivotal change in the American civil rights movement. Far from being merely a weary seamstress, as the myth often portrays her, Parks was an educated activist—secretary of the Montgomery chapter of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP)—who intentionally made a stand that evening, fully aware of its possible ramifications. She was arrested and fined for violating Montgomery's segregation policies by refusing to yield her seat to a white passenger, but her arrest would lead to unforeseen consequences.

Days after the incident, local activists, led by Jo Ann Robinson of the Women's Political Council, began to circulate and print around 35,000 flyers urging a one-day boycott of the buses on December 5, 1955. The boycott was so effective that a group of community leaders created the Montgomery Improvement Association to organize further efforts, and elected a 26-year-old pastor, Martin Luther King Jr., as their president. The boycott, initially sparked by the issue of bus segregation, evolved into a 381-day movement where approximately 40,000 Black residents in Montgomery opted to walk, carpool, and suffer intimidation and violence rather than use the segregated buses. Despite the bombing of King's house and the dismissal or arrest of many who participated in the boycott, the community remained steadfast.

On December 20, 1956, the boycott was finally over when the Supreme Court affirmed the lower court's decision in Browder v. Gayle, declaring bus segregation unconstitutional. This was a significant win, proving that mass, nonviolent protest and organization could effectively break down barriers of institutional discrimination. The success of the Montgomery Bus Boycott also launched King onto the national stage, leading to the establishment of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference in 1957.

The Montgomery Bus Boycott is a crucial episode in civil rights history not only because of the specific legal win it secured, but also for setting a precedent for how activism would unfold in the coming decade. It illustrated that individuals, such as domestic workers, teachers, and students, could mobilize in a disciplined, collective manner to combat an unjust system. While Rosa Parks's bravery ignited the spark, it was the steadfast resolve of Montgomery's Black community that fueled the flame. As Parks later acknowledged, "the only tired I was, was tired of giving in." Her arrest and the movement she set off proved that resistance to injustice could start with a simple refusal to move.

In June 2013, 29-year-old Booz Allen Hamilton contractor Edward Snowden, stationed at the National Security Agency (NSA) facility in Hawaii, leaked to journalists Glenn Greenwald and Laura Poitras thousands of classified documents exposing programs including PRISM and bulk data collection of U.S. phone records under Section 215 of the Patriot Act. These revelations, first reported by The Guardian on June 6, 2013, ignited a global conversation about surveillance, privacy, and the limits of state secrecy. It also raised a more difficult question: in what circumstances, if any, is it ethical to violate a sworn oath and the law in order to disclose wrongdoing?

Snowden's defense pivots on the ethics of consequences and the call of conscience. He exposed the NSA's collection of metadata from millions of U.S. citizens without individualized suspicion. Later in the year, a federal judge, Richard Leon, described this as "almost Orwellian." The importance of whistleblowing in cases like this comes from the often-inadequate internal mechanisms for redress. Snowden has claimed he voiced concerns internally, but felt that any formal complaints would be suppressed or weaponized. From a utilitarian ethical perspective, one could argue his decision was justifiable because the negative consequences of disclosure were outweighed by the positive outcomes of accountability, public discourse, and, ultimately, reform (such as the USA FREEDOM Act of 2015, which ended the bulk collection of phone records).

On the other hand, Snowden committed a violation of the Espionage Act of 1917. He had sworn an oath to safeguard classified material. He fled first to Hong Kong and then to Moscow, where he has resided since 2013. Is his action driven solely by principle or was it motivated in part by personal interests? Deontological ethics would argue that there is an intrinsic moral value to adhering to rules and promises. When an intelligence agent makes an independent judgment about what secrets the public should be privy to, this creates a dangerous precedent that could threaten lives or disrupt essential security operations. Some, including former NSA Director Michael Hayden, have criticized Snowden by pointing out that he could have used legal mechanisms (such as the Intelligence Community Whistleblower Protection Act), even if flawed.

This ethical dilemma is difficult to solve because it involves a clash between two important values: the importance of law and institutional trust versus the public's need for information when a government acts in secret beyond its own bounds. The Snowden affair raises the possibility that whistleblowing may be morally justified only in very specific circumstances: where wrongdoing is systemic and the negative consequences significant, and where internal procedures are exhausted. By this measure, Snowden's actions may not represent treason or heroism, but a calculated risk that the truth is worth the known consequences.

Summary
 In June 2013, 29-year-old National Security Agency employee (and Booz Allen Hamilton contractor) Edward Snowden shared thousands of sensitive documents with journalists Glenn Greenwald and Laura Poitras revealing programs such as PRISM and mass collection of US phone data (under the Patriot Act, Section 215). First reported by The Guardian on June 6, 2013, these revelations sparked an international discussion on surveillance, privacy, and state secrecy, and perhaps more fundamentally, raised the question: is there ever a situation where it's acceptable to break an oath and the law to disclose wrongdoing?

On one hand, Snowden is a case for consequences and conscience. He exposed that the NSA was gathering metadata from millions of Americans without individual suspicion. (In a later decision from later that year, a federal judge Richard Leon described this as "almost Orwellian.") Whistleblowing is significant because institutional avenues can be ineffective; Snowden has argued he discussed the issues with coworkers and felt complaints would be ignored or used against him. Defending Snowden's decision can also be justified from a utilitarian perspective, wherein the negative consequences of the exposure were outweighed by the public good of accountability, discussion, and eventually reform (like with the USA FREEDOM Act of 2015, which ended the mass phone data program).

On the other hand, Snowden is a serious case for wrongdoing. Snowden broke the Espionage Act of 1917. He took an oath to protect classified information. He fled to Hong Kong and then Russia, where he has resided since 2013. It begs the question: was it pure principle or self-preservation? For deontological arguments, rules and promises have moral significance. Making an unilateral judgement about what the public "ought to know" in an intelligence officer sets a dangerous precedent that could threaten lives or hinder legitimate security operations. Critics (like former NSA head Michael Hayden) contended that Snowden had legal options, like the Intelligence Community Whistleblower Protection Act, though they may not have been perfect.

The Snowden dilemma is difficult to neatly resolve because it presents two important goods in conflict: the rule of law and trust in institutions versus the public's interest to know when a government crosses its own lines, secretly. Snowden's example does seem to imply that whistleblowing is only justifiable in a narrow set of situations: large-scale wrongdoing, significant harm, and that the institutional avenues have been thoroughly explored. By these metrics, Snowden's decision seems to be more an informed risk-taking strategy that the truth was worth the known consequences, rather than treason or an act of heroism.

Gatsby is often seen reaching for the small green light that's on the end of the dock at Daisy's house. Nick Carraway eventually comes to the understanding that Gatsby's dream is simply one born of fantasy in his idealized remembrance. In F. Scott Fitzgerald's 1925 novel The Great Gatsby, the green light at the end of the dock of Daisy Buchanan represents Jay Gatsby's dreams and, in particular, his desire to be with Daisy again and to bring back the past relationship he once had with her. Nick Carraway eventually understands that Gatsby's dream is more of a memory of something that was ideal rather than actual. What Gatsby wants is not just to be with Daisy in 1922.
