The catastrophic failure of Napoleon's 1812 Russian Campaign was not something inevitable, but a series of decisions, first and foremost made by Napoleon himself. Napoleon's decision to invade Russia was tied to a political disagreement which was not, by any means, worth such a war. Russia's Tsar Alexander I stopped participating in Napoleon's Continental System (blockade of Britain) because the system was suffocating Russia's trade in items such as wood and tallow. Instead of trying to negotiate or compromise on the issue, Napoleon instead massed a Grande Armée of about 600,000, the largest army Europe had ever seen, and marched across the Neman River on June 24, 1812.

1) The campaign was a preventable disaster at numerous junctures. First, the decision to launch an invasion late in June was foolhardy. Napoleon took a chance that he could force a decisive battle and force Alexander into peace within a few weeks. But the Russians, first under Barclay de Tolly and later under Mikhail Kutuzov, did not let themselves be cornered and instead pulled back to the east and burned supplies as they went. The campaign was a 'run and catch' affair with no decisive victory. Napoleon arrived in Moscow in September. He had to win (and pay the price for) the Battle of Borodino, September 7, which killed around 70,000 people on both sides, before he arrived in Moscow only to see it burning and Alexander unwilling to negotiate. A man as intelligent as Napoleon should have had plans in case something like this happened, but instead he stayed in Moscow for a month and a half waiting for a letter that never arrived, before winter forced a retreat.

2) The army's logistics were deliberately insufficient. Napoleon's plan was to supply the army, in part, from magazines, and in part to forage for food, but the Russian scorched-earth policy and the distance made this impossible. Tens of thousands of horses died; the army was ravaged by typhus and dysentery before a single major battle had taken place. It's estimated that out of the 600,000 that went into Russia, fewer than 100,000 made it out. Had Napoleon sent a smaller army with proper logistical support, or had he planned a limited operation targeting Lithuania and Belorussia, it might have been possible to negotiate peace and avoid the disaster.

Napoleon apologists will claim that, as hegemon of Europe, Napoleon had to enforce the Continental System and that if Russia was allowed to rebel, Austria and Prussia could defect. This is partly true, but it doesn't excuse the way the invasion was carried out. Alternative ways of pressuring diplomatically, threatening them in Poland, even planning a limited but punitive operation, could have been an alternative.

Ultimately, the invasion was a preventable disaster due to overconfidence, lack of intelligence, and Napoleon's failure to realize that an enemy might just not want to play his game. Russia didn't so much 'beat' Napoleon on the battlefield as it beat him with his own assumptions.

The defeat Napoleon suffered in 1812 in Russia was not a foregone conclusion, it was a failure based on a series of decisions, most significantly those taken by Napoleon himself. The invasion itself began with a political dispute that really wasn't worth the scale of the war that followed: Tsar Alexander I of Russia left the Continental System (the British blockade by Napoleon) because it was starving Russian trade (of timber, tallow, etc.) of European goods. Napoleon, instead of pursuing a diplomatic solution, or at least a compromise, mobilized the Grande Armée (about 600,000 soldiers, the biggest army Europe had ever seen), and crossed the Neman River on June 24, 1812. 
 The whole catastrophe can be seen in terms of the way in which it could have been avoided. First, the timing was disastrous. Napoleon invaded late in June, hoping to draw the Russians into a single, decisive battle and make Alexander come to terms within a few weeks' time. When the Russians (under Barclay de Tolly first, then Kutuzov Mikhail) wouldn't be cornered, and instead fell back eastwards while burning stores, it was a cat-and-mouse chase with no real victories. By September, Napoleon had made it to Moscow (along the way, the expensive Battle of Borodino on Sept. 7, with about 70k casualties on both sides), and found the city on fire, and Alexander not willing to negotiate. Any emperor as smart as Napoleon would have had contingency plans for this kind of eventuality, but instead he sat in Moscow for over a month, waiting for a letter that never came, until winter finally forced his retreat. 
 Second, Napoleon chose to know that his logistics were not up to the task. He wanted his army to be sustained both by magazines and by foraging, but the Russian scorched-earth policy and the vast distances involved made that impossible. Tens of thousands of horses perished; typhus and dysentery decimated troops before the first major battle was even fought. Historians think that of the 600k men who went into Russia, only about 100k came out. A less ambitious force with guaranteed supply lines, or a restricted campaign limited to Lithuania and Belorussia, could have led to negotiated settlement without the disaster. 
 Pro-Napoleon historians might try to make the point that as hegemon of Europe, Napoleon had to enforce the Continental System, and to let Russia flout it would invite defections from Austria and Prussia. There's some merit to this, but it's not a defense of the execution of the invasion as much as of the motive. There were alternatives, like applying diplomatic pressure, or staging a show of strength in Poland, or even a more limited punitive expedition. 
 The invasion could have been avoided: it was a disaster due to a combination of overconfidence, lack of intelligence, and Napoleon's inability to conceive that any opponent might just... not want to play his game. It wasn't so much the Russians who beat Napoleon, but his own preconceptions.

On November 9, 1989, during a press conference, a mistake was made by Günter Schabowski, spokesman of the East German government. In announcing new travel regulations, he accidentally said they'd be effective "immediately," when in reality the East German authorities wanted to permit a slow, gradual opening up of the borders. At border-crossing points such as the Bornholmer Strasse, masses of people gathered. The border guards had no instructions and, in sheer confusion, started allowing people to pass. In no time, thousands of East and West Berliners were dancing on the Wall around the Brandenburg Gate. They broke off pieces of the Wall using hammers.

The fall of the Berlin Wall wasn't so much an unexpected accident but rather the result of years of mounting tension. The glasnost and perestroika reforms of Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev had started to reduce Moscow's control over the Eastern bloc. By 1989, Gorbachev announced that the Soviet Union was not going to intervene militarily to support satellite states like in Hungary (1956) or Czechoslovakia (1968). As early as May, the border fence between Hungary and Austria was demolished, allowing the East Germans a new channel to escape to the west.

Meanwhile, massive protests were taking place in East Germany. The Monday protests in Leipzig reached more than 70,000 in October 9. In early November, East Berlin crowds numbered over 500,000. Hardline leader Erich Honecker, in power in East Germany since 1971, resigned in mid-October. His successor, Egon Krenz, could not stem the tide.

The repercussions of the fall of the Berlin Wall were immediate and profound. By October 3, 1990, less than a year later, Germany was formally reunified under Chancellor Helmut Kohl. The fall of the Berlin Wall also hastened the fall of the communist governments in the Eastern Bloc. Within weeks, the Velvet Revolution in Czechoslovakia was successful. By December 1989, the brutal regime of Nicolae Ceaușescu was toppled in Romania.

The reunification cost a lot of money. Trillions of deutsche marks had to be transferred to modernize the eastern part. Decades later, economists are still discussing this.

In political terms, the fall of the Berlin Wall was seen as the symbolic end of the Cold War. It was formally ended when the Soviet Union disintegrated in December 1991. A bureaucratic gaffe during a press conference led to one of the most important historical ruptures of the 20th century.

On the evening of November 9, 1989, East German spokesperson Günter Schabowski inadvertently announced that new travel rules would apply "immediately," but authorities had actually planned for a slow, managed release of border restrictions. Large numbers of people rushed to crossing points such as Bornholmer Strasse. The beleaguered border troops, without clear instructions, began admitting people. Soon, thousands of East and West Berliners were on the top of the Wall near the Brandenburg Gate, using hammers to break off pieces.

The fall of the Berlin Wall was not a random occurrence but the outcome of a process building over several years. In 1989, the policies of glasnost and perestroika initiated by Mikhail Gorbachev in Moscow eased Soviet control over Eastern Europe. Furthermore, in 1989 he indicated that Soviet Union would not send troops to shore up satellite states militarily, as it had in Hungary in 1956 or Czechoslovakia in 1968. That May, the border fence between Hungary and Austria had been torn down. This created a new possibility for East Germans to escape to the West. In addition, large-scale demonstrations took place in East Germany itself. For example, the Monday demonstrations in Leipzig reached over 70,000 people by October 9, and by early November demonstrations in East Berlin had swelled to over half a million. Erich Honecker, the hardline leader of East Germany since 1971, was forced out of office in mid-October. His successor Egon Krenz could not stem the tide.

The implications of the fall of the Berlin Wall were immediate and sweeping. On October 3, 1990, under the leadership of Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Germany was formally reunified, less than a year after the Berlin Wall fell. The fall of the Berlin Wall also hastened the demise of communist regimes throughout the Eastern Bloc. For example, Czechoslovakia underwent a "velvet revolution" in a matter of weeks. By December 1989, Nicolae Ceaușescu's regime in Romania had been violently overthrown. Reunification of Germany had an economic cost. Trillions of deutsche marks were transferred to upgrade the former East. This subject is still being discussed by economists decades after the fall of the Berlin Wall. Symbolically, the fall of the Berlin Wall is often cited as the final blow in the Cold War. It became official when the Soviet Union itself broke apart in December 1991. A simple, bureaucratic error during a press conference was one of the great turning points of the 20th century.

Driving for Uber felt like freedom in 2020. But during the COVID-19 pandemic we saw how freedom can easily lead to exploitation. With Uber, you had the freedom to work when you wanted to work, turn down rides, and make money on the app without a boss. If you lost your job at a restaurant, store, or office, that could be valuable. But you also had to pay for gas and your car. And for repairs. And for insurance. And for your time waiting for riders, when you weren't getting paid. You were an independent contractor, so typically you didn't have sick leave, unemployment, or health care provided by your employer.

When travel plummeted during lockdowns in March and April 2020, the dangers increased. Uber said its rides business was down roughly 80 percent year over year in April. At the same time, drivers were still at risk of spreading the coronavirus from one person to the next. Uber offered $24 million to help drivers and delivery people around the world, but the aid was scarce and hard to access for many people. The company mandated mask use and new safety measures, sometimes outsourcing the responsibility of staying safe to the driver.

The issue flared up in California. The 2019 law, Assembly Bill 5, made it more difficult for firms to claim that their employees were contractors. Uber and Lyft told us drivers like to be free, and they mounted a big campaign to pass Proposition 22. On November 3, 2020, California voters voted for Proposition 22. It kept drivers on app-based platforms as independent contractors, with modest benefits like a healthcare subsidy and pay for time spent driving when engaged. Those in favor, like Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, said that drivers were getting the flexibility they wanted. Those opposed said that a profitable tech company should not be able to dodge the costs of employment.

So Uber drivers were experiencing both freedom and exploitation in 2020. They could control their hours on the app. But not their fares. And not their expenses. And not the health risks. And not the benefits. You really want flexibility as a driver. So you want to continue controlling your hours. But you also need more protection from getting sick or getting into a crash or dealing with income insecurity. 2020 taught us that being independent doesn't matter much if the worker has to bear almost all the risk and the company still has most of the control.

Uber driving in 2020 appeared to be the epitome of freedom. But thanks to the COVID-19 pandemic, it became clear that that freedom was also exploitation. As an Uber driver, you can set your own hours, turn down rides, and make money with your own smartphone app—without a boss in the traditional sense. This flexibility can be very valuable, particularly for those who’ve lost jobs as restaurant workers or retail and office staff.

And yet you must pay for gas and car maintenance. You must pay for car insurance. You must sit idle waiting for riders and not get paid. You’re categorized as an independent contractor, so you don’t usually get paid sick leave or unemployment insurance. And you’re not eligible for employer-provided health care coverage.

It’s particularly risky in March and April of 2020, as lockdowns cause a precipitous drop in mobility. Uber says its rides business had an 80 percent year-over-year drop in April, and you’re still possibly infecting riders with coronavirus as you drive them around. Sure, Uber offers $24 million in aid for drivers and delivery personnel around the world. But that aid is scarce and hard for many to access. And Uber has mandatory mask wearing and safety protocols. But that still puts some of the onus on individual drivers to protect themselves.

The contest plays out in California particularly clearly, thanks to the passage of Assembly Bill 5 in 2019. That law made it more difficult for companies to treat their workers as independent contractors. Uber and Lyft say drivers care about being independent, so they’ve made a big push for the passage of Proposition 22. In California, on November 3, 2020, voters passed that proposition, which lets app drivers stay independent contractors, but which offers them some benefits—at least a healthcare subsidy, and pay for time driving engaged. Supporters of the law, including Uber’s CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, say it allows for the flexibility that drivers want. Others say it lets successful tech companies off the hook for the costs of employment.

Uber drivers in 2020 were therefore both free and exploited. They had control over their time through the app. But they didn’t have control over their fares. Or their costs. Or their health risks. Or their access to benefits. For real flexibility, you want drivers to continue to have their autonomy about their time. But they also want better protection from illness, or accidents, or the uncertainty of their income. The big takeaway of 2020 is that autonomy isn’t so great when you’re almost completely on the hook for all risks while companies enjoy most of the power.

The haunting that lingers beyond emancipation as a trauma of slavery in Toni Morrison's Beloved (1987) is a remembrance that lingers in the present as an almost ghostly presence like the ghost inhabiting 124 Bluestone Road. Beloved centers on Sethe, a runaway slave in 1873 Cincinnati 18 years after her escape from the Sweet Home plantation in Kentucky. But Sethe, the runaway slave, is unable to forget the ghost of the past that continually returns as what Sethe calls "rememory." Morrison's creation of the word "rememory" implies that memories are not personal property but are an inhabiting force - they live in the world, and they lie in wait to surprise the unwary. Denver must be careful, Sethe warns her, because even if Denver forgets the shame of Sweet Home, "it's still out there." It is a place where the past can still happen to you.

The novel's primary horror, Sethe's 1855 murder of her two year old daughter to stop her from being returned to slavery as a slave, is deliberately kept from the reader as fragments until it is revealed. This approximates how actual traumatic memories function. Sethe is unable to tell the story of what happened in linear order and she cannot. The experience keeps coming back in fragments evoked by the senses. When Beloved physically appears at 124 as though Sethe's dead daughter has come back at the age she would have been at (about nineteen), Morrison takes the concept of the past refusing to remain buried and makes it literal. Beloved literally devours Sethe's stories. Beloved wants to hear them repeatedly, even though the act of telling and remembering is nearly driving the teller mad.

At the same time, Morrison emphasizes the importance, even though painful, of the necessity of memory. The fact that the community has left Sethe alone - as represented by Baby Suggs's deserted sermons in the Clearing - leaves the ghost able to grow, and only when thirty women come to 124 to sing and pray is Beloved exorcised. Paul D's final realization that Sethe's love was "too thick" and his vow to rub her feet seem to point to the way that the healing may lie in the shared remembrance instead of isolation. The dedication of the novel to "Sixty Million and more" indicates that Sethe's story is a representative of the suppressed collective history. In fashioning a narrative of what was unspeakable, Morrison suggests that it is not possible for a people to progress without first facing the events. Literature can be an act of remembrance. Beloved concludes with the statement "This is not a story to pass on." It is a paradox - both it should not be told again but also it should not be passed over, forgotten or ignored.

In Toni Morrison's Beloved (1987), she portrays the effects of slavery trauma, which goes beyond its emancipation and continues as a memory that haunts the present, like the ghost in 124 Bluestone Road. The escaped slave Sethe is now in Cincinnati, in 1873, eighteen years after she escaped from the Sweet Home plantation in Kentucky. But the escaped slave cannot shake what she calls "rememory," what keeps haunting her. By coining this term, Morrison indicates the memories are not merely ours but occupy us, existing in the world itself to waylay whoever happens to walk by. Sethe cautions Denver even if she forgets the disgrace of Sweet Home, it's still there. It's a place where the past can happen to you.

The awful thing that Sethe did, the murder of her 2-year old daughter in 1855 to prevent the child from being re-enslaved, is intentionally withheld from the reader and presented piecemeal - much like the way traumatic memories really function. Sethe can't recount the story in a linear manner - she can't. But it comes in fragments. It is set off by sensory details. When Beloved appears in the flesh at 124 (apparently the dead daughter resurrected at the age she would have been, around 19) Morrison makes the metaphor literal. The past will not stay dead. Beloved voraciously feeds on Sethe's stories. She wants them repeated over and over again, until the teller and the rememberer almost fall apart.

But Morrison maintains that memory, while painful, is also necessary. The fact that Sethe was abandoned by the community (exemplified by the abandoned sermons of Baby Suggs in the Clearing), contributed to the blooming of the ghost. It takes thirty women coming to 124 to sing and pray, before Beloved can be exorcized. Finally, when Paul D understands that Sethe's love was "too thick" and promises to rub her feet, the idea is that rather than isolation, it is mutual remembrance that will be the path to healing. In the dedication - "Sixty Million and more" - Morrison makes it clear that the story of Sethe represents a collective story that has been kept down. By putting narrative to what was unutterable, Morrison states that a people cannot progress until they confront what has happened. And that literature can be a form of remembrance. The final statement of Beloved - "This is not a story to pass on" is a paradox. On the one hand, the story should not be repeated. But on the other, the story should not be passed over, or forgotten or ignored.

It’s completely normal for a newby to get that acetone (nailpolish remover) smell! It means it’s fermenting, not dying! 
 What’s going on: after ~48-72 hours, the wild yeast & bacteria in your flour are producing acetic acid and esters as they eat through the starches. As the starter gets low on food between feedings, the bacteria will change it’s game and start putting out some acetone-y smells. This is especially true with whole grain flours like rye or whole wheat as they ferment faster/harder than your typical AP flour. 
 How to fix: 
 1. Feed it more often. For the next 3-4 days, try feeding every 12 hours instead of every 24 hours. You want to do a 1:1:1 weight ratio (50g starter : 50g flour : 50g water ~78f) 
 2. Are you diluting it too much? If it’s too thin, the acids build up faster. Slightly thicker (equal parts by weight) will slow it down. 
 3. Is your counter warmer than 75f (near oven/warm kitchen)? This can speed up the fermentation and make it eat all it’s food faster. Try to keep between 68-75f. I put mine next to my coffee maker (not near stove) and it made a HUGE difference. 
 What happens: often, day 4-6 it can actually start smelling worse. Like gym socks or vomit. It’s different bacterial populations duking it out. Don’t freak out! Don’t throw it away. By days 7-10, most starters will start to have a pleasant yeasty/slightly tangy/apple cider vinegar smell. It will also start to rise reliably (doubles 4-6 hours after a feed) 
 When to really worry: if you see pink/orange streaks (mold) or furry stuff on top. Not to worry just because it smells like acetone. It’s just hungry. Stick to a consistent feeding schedule and it’ll be fine. 
 source: I’ve been working on the same starter since march 2021. It smelled like a nail salon every time I forgot to feed it for a day too long 😅

datetime.utcnow() (and utcfromtimestamp()) are, by definition, a naive datetime. It provides UTC wall times, but clears away the tzinfo so it is not clear that it is UTC.  It was deprecated in 3.12 because it is too easy to do the following: Take this naive datetime object, assume it's a local time, and end up with silent errors when you compare to an aware datetime or call astimezone() on it.

Instead, don't use utcnow() at all. Build an aware datetime:

    from datetime import datetime, timezone

    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

Now, now has tzinfo=timezone.utc. So now.isoformat() is going to return 2026-09-21T14:32:07.512983+00:00, not a naked 2026-09-21T14:32:07.512983 which could be anything. (If you're on 3.11+, datetime.UTC is a convenient shortcut for timezone.utc)

2024+ things you should also do:

* don't compare naive and aware datetimes. Python will throw a TypeError: can't compare offset naive and offset aware datetimes.  This is nice because Python doesn't just silently do the wrong thing.  But you have to do this consistently.
* if you want anything other than just UTC, and you need say America/Chicago or Asia/Tokyo.  Use the standard library zoneinfo instead of pytz (3.9+).

    from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
    chicago = datetime.now(ZoneInfo("America/Chicago"))

* store your timestamps in UTC (aware or explicit utc-naive, just be consistent), in your db.  Only convert to a local timezone at your display time.
* If you are using Django and you have USE_TZ=True, and you are using django.utils.timezone.now() this is all already correct and has the same pattern.

So in summary, the non-deprecated direct replacement to datetime.utcnow() is datetime.now(timezone.utc)

datetime.utcnow() (or utcfromtimestamp()) produces a naive datetime.  By design, it's returning you the wall-clock time in UTC, but without tzinfo which means it's not "tagged" as being UTC.

So... this is exactly why it's been deprecated in 3.12 because it's very easy to then take that naive datetime, think it's a localtime, and then do silly things like compare it with an aware datetime or attempt to use astimezone() on it - which would then give you silent incorrect results.

Instead, you need to move away from using utcnow() altogether and instead create an aware datetime:

from datetime import datetime, timezone

now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

now will then have tzinfo=timezone.utc.  So when you do now.isoformat(), you'll get '2026-09-21T14:32:07.512983+00:00' and not just '2026-09-21T14:32:07.512983' which is ambiguous.

Also note that datetime.UTC in 3.11+ is an alias for timezone.utc

Other things you should be doing for 2024+ code:

- Don't mix naive and aware datetimes when comparing them (Python will throw TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes.  Which is good.  But...  it means you need to be consistent).
- If you're not just interested in UTC time but also other timeszones (e.g. America/Chicago or Asia/Tokyo) then instead of using pytz, you can use the stdlib's zoneinfo (3.9+) like this:

from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
chicago = datetime.now(ZoneInfo("America/Chicago"))

- You should be storing timestamps in your database as UTC (aware or explicit-utc-naive but consistent), then just converting to your local timezone at the display layer.
- If using Django, then USE_TZ=True with django.utils.timezone.now() already does the right thing and is doing this same thing.

So datetime.now(timezone.utc) is the direct/not-deprecated replacement for datetime.utcnow().

 2) Tax buffer: For quarterly federal & state estimated tax payments

Could be a number of things. Grinding for an 09 Civic in particular can be traced back to a few things. 
 Most likely would be: Worn out brake pads. Especially for the time frame (06-11) front pads are a common service interval for Civics. At ~40-60k miles usually. If your pads are worn down to the metal backing you'll get grinding and the downhill aspect is due to the fact that you're applying more brake pressure for longer periods of time and therefore generating more heat and pressure. So, if it grinds when you apply the brakes this is your first suspect. Pull a wheel off or look through the spokes. You want to see at least 3mm of pad friction material on the pad. If you see grooves and a scored face on the rotor you've been riding metal on metal a while and you'll need new rotors as well. Expect to pay around $150-250 per axle in an independent shop for pads and rotors. 
 Why downhill? a few reasons 
 1. Heat. When you're on an extended downhill and doing extended braking (think long grade) this generates heat to the rotors. If the rotors are warped and/or uneven deposits are on the rotor then you can get a pulsing feel as well as a groaning or grinding noise. If the rotors are warped it's usually because pads were not taken care of at some point during the life of the car. 
 2. Weight transfer. When you're braking downhill, you're putting more force into the front brakes. If the pads or rotors are worn then you're going to hear that more. 
 Other potential: 
 -Glazed pads. If the previous owner abused the brakes and was riding them then the pad surface can harden up. Which can cause a grinding/growling under load. 
 -Stuck caliper. Stuck caliper slide pin can be a thing on 8th gen Civics. A pin can seize and drag the pad on the rotor causing a grinding. Especially if it's hot. Does one wheel look a lot dustier or hotter than the others after driving? 
 -Rust on rotors. If the car sits days at a time, it can cause surface rust that makes a noise. Typically that will go away after a couple stops. But if it makes a constant grinding noise, that's not it. 
 You don't want to procrastinate. Grinding = metal contact. So for each week you leave this unchecked you're wearing down the rotors and could be leading to more damage like calipers. Pads and rotors on a Civic is a very easy DIY. Assuming you have the skill for it. It's easily doable in 2hrs with basic tools. If not, take it to a shop ASAP this week. 
 Quick test. Does it only grind when you apply the brakes? Or does it make the grinding noise when coasting downhill without applying brake pressure? If you have noise when coasting downhill, it's most likely a wheel bearing or caliper drag. This will be big info for your mechanic.

No. This confuses a lot of people because of recent rule changes (2018). 
If you're W2 "working remotely for my employer" implies you're a W2 employee. Due to TCJA (Tax Cuts Jobs Act) there is a suspension on miscellaneous itemized deduction for unreimbursed employee business expenses (like home office) for tax years 2018 through 2025. So if you're working 1 day a week from home or 5 days a week. The key is that you're a W2 employee so you cannot deduct this on your federal return period. Doesn't matter if you're required by your employer to have this hybrid schedule and you don't get your permanent desk on the days you're in. 
What could influence this answer? 
1. If you are a 1099 contractor or have self employment income as well. You can take a deduction for the home business use of your home for that income (i.e. you freelance consult or something from your home office). You would use Form 8829 for this. Of course, your home office must meet "regular and exclusive use" test. Meaning, your home office can't be your home office and a guest room on weekends for example. 
2. State Taxes. There are a few states that still allow unreimbursed employee expense deductions on state return even with federal suspension (California, New York, Pennsylvania, Alabama, Arkansas). You can check specific rules for 2025 in your state. 
3. If your employer doesn't reimburse you for this. You'd need to see if they have "accountable plan". If they reimburse you some amount for internet, monitor, etc. And it's under accountable plan then that reimbursement is not taxable to you (effectively even better than a deduction). 
So for typical hybrid W2 employee no home office deduction on federal. Look at your state. Ask if your employer will reimburse you for this expense. 
This is not tax advice for your specific situation. Ask a CPA to see if you can do this from your complete return.

If the hole is 2 inches, skip the attempt at filling with joint compound. Instead, go to your hardware store and pick up a self adhesive metal drywall patch.

First, cut off any loose paper. Use a utility knife to clean up the ragged edges (get it to square up). Clean off the dust.

Place a metal mesh patch (4 inches or larger) in the center of the hole. Press down so that it is completely flat. If the damage is close to a corner or stud be sure not to place the patch across any uneven surface.

Fill the patch with setting joint compound (like 45-minute Easy Sand). Use a 6-inch taping knife. Feather the compound at least 3 inches outside of the patch. Allow to set. Remove any ridges. Apply a second coat of compound (thinner). You may need a third skim coat to fully cover the patch.

After the final coat is dry (overnight usually) lightly sand with 150 or 220 grit sand paper. Run your hand across the surface. If you feel an edge don't sand like mad. Instead, apply more compound. Clean off the dust. Prime your repair with drywall primer. Paint with the same color as your wall.

Since it was a door knob, you will want to put on a doorstop (or a hinge pin stop) after you repair it. If your knob is banging into the wall a rubber wall mount stop will typically be the best choice. If your hole is close to an electrical outlet or switch turn off the circuit before you cut or sand. Also, don't drive any screws in the area.

If you have a 2-in hole, don't try to just fill the hole with joint compound. Get a self stick metal patch for dry wall and use that.

Step 1. First, remove any loose paper and clean up ragged edges with utility knife. Get rid of dust.

Step 2. You'll want to get a patch in the form of metal mesh, 4 in or larger. Center it over the hole and firmly push it flat. If you've got a hole near a corner or stud, just be sure it's not bridging an uneven surface.

Step 3. Top the patch with setting type joint compound (like 45 min Easy Sand). Use a 6 in taping knife and feather out the compound at least 3 in from the patch. Allow to harden, then scrape off any ridges. Apply a thinner second coat. You might need a skim third coat for total concealment of patch.

Step 4. Once final coat is dry (usually overnight), lightly sand the surface with 150/220 sandpaper. Feel it with your hand. If it's got an edge to it, apply more compound instead of going at it with sandpaper. Clean dust away. Prime repair with dry wall primer. Paint with matching wall color.

Since you have a hole caused by door knob, you'll want to add door stop or hinge pin stop after you repair it. In the case of a knob that touches the wall, you'll probably want a wall mounted rubber stop. If you're close to an outlet or switch, you'll want to turn off the circuit for cutting/sanding. Avoid screws in that area.

Good news, 120/80 is a very healthy number at 55. In fact it's pretty much the gold standard. 
 For reference, anything below 120/80 is 'normal' according to the american heart association. 
 120-129 systolic and < 80 diastolic is 'elevated'. 
 Stage 1 hypertension is 130/80. 
 Stage 2 hypertension is 140/90. 
 You're basically at the upper end of the 'normal' range. Which is where most 55 year old people who are healthy will be. 
 As people age, their BP can rise due to blood vessels becoming stiffer. Being 120/80 at the middle of your 50's is a good thing. Not a cause for alarm. 
 
 However, a few things to consider: 
 1. A single number isn't a diagnosis. 
 Your BP will fluctuate depending on the time of day and stress level. Caffeine consumption, sleep. Even speaking during BP measurement. If your 120/80 was from a single reading at say a drug store machine or a stressful visit to your doctor's office. Then take a few more measurements at home (seated, arm supported. Resting for 5 minutes) over a week or two and see what your average number is. 
 
 2. Ask about your 10 year risk, not just your BP number. 
 With your age (55) your doctor should be looking at your cholesterol, blood glucose, family history, smoking, weight. 
 You could have good BP and a higher risk due to other factors. 
 
 3. Continue monitoring. 
 It's recommended you check it at least once a year during your physical. Or more often if you have a family history of high BP. 
 
 Of course. In order to maintain your BP it's recommended you moderate sodium intake (under 2300mg/day ideally under 1500mg/day). Exercise (aerobic at least 150 minutes per week). Moderate alcohol. Watch your weight. 
 
 No. It's not something you need to be worried about. It's a number most 55 year olds would be pleased to have. 
 Mention it at your next check up. Continue to monitor for trends. Because trends are more important than a single number. 
 
 *standard disclaimer. I'm not a doctor. If you're experiencing any symptoms such as headaches, dizziness, chest discomfort. See your doc regardless of your numbers.*

best thing is baking soda paste.  Takes about 10 minutes.

If it is still stinky,  use coarse salt for a scrubbing.  spread salt down on board. (the same things that break down and cause garlic breath, allicin compounds).  The salt will pull up the crap that's in the wood grain.  Rinse and dry. 
 
 For really bad things like months of soaking up garlic and onion smell, you can also let it sit in a 1T baking soda quart of warm water.  Sit in the water (or in paste) for 15-20 minutes and then scrub with a stiff bristled brush with the grain. 
 
 
 Avoid: 
 a) putting your wood board in dishwasher or sitting for hours soaking.  (especially end grain boards - they'll crack or delaminate) 
 
 b) Don't use just vinegar.  That will slowly rob wood of its natural oils with repeated use.  It's ok to use it occasionally.  mix it 1:1 with water.  Wipe and rinse quickly. 
 
 c) once dry,  rub in a mineral oil (food safe).  or a board cream (bees wax and mineral oil).  this will recondition the wood and it will actually be more resistant next time.  more oil = less porous. 
 
 if you're a big garlic cutter - try to have a little board just for pungent foods and not get this problem on your main board.

Most effective way is a baking soda paste. Can do in about 10 minutes. 
 1) 3:1 baking soda to water paste (3Tbsp to 1Tbsp for a typical 18" board) 
 2) Rub into the board using a clean cloth or the cut side of a lemon (moving with the grain) Allow to sit for 5-10 minutes. 
 3) Rinse with hot water then immediately dry. (Stand on end to prevent warping) 
 
If you're still smelling it, use coarse salt as a physical scrub (spread over board, then use half lemon with salt as an abrasive to scrub) the salt loosens the muck from the wood grain. The citric acid breaks down the sulfur compounds that cause "sticking" (i.e. the same allicin breakdown products that cause garlic breath). Rinse & dry 
 
If you've had a board absorbing garlic/onion for months, try a longer soak - dissolve 1 Tbsp baking soda in quart of warm water. Let board sit submerged (or coated in the paste) for 15-20 minutes then scrub with a stiff brush (against the grain) 
 
Don't use a wood board in the dishwasher, don't soak for extended period (especially end grain boards. They will crack/delaminate). 
 
Don't use straight vinegar first. That may deaden the natural oils in the wood after repeated use. Not bad occasionally in 1:1 dilution with water, wiped and rinsed quickly. 
 
Once dry, use a food grade mineral oil or board cream (beewax/mineral oil mix). This conditions the board, and actually makes it less likely to smell the next time you use it (because now the surface is not as porous as it was once well-oiled). 
 
If you're chopping garlic a lot, have a small board dedicated just to the garlicy stuff so you won't have this problem on your main board.

Given a table `users` with an `email` column, group on email (group if more than 1):

SELECT
    email
,   COUNT(*) as duplicate_count
FROM users
WHERE email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY duplicate_count DESC, email;

The above will show you each email that's duplicated along with how many. For example, if alex@example.com is duplicated 3 times it will show:

alex@example.com | 3

Now if you want to consider email addresses duplicated regardless of case or even white space around them, you'd normalize those in your query.

SELECT
    LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS normalized_email
,   COUNT(*) as duplicate_count
FROM users
WHERE email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY duplicate_count DESC;

If you want to know which users are associated with these emails you can do a derived table:

SELECT u.*
FROM users u
JOIN (
    SELECT
        LOWER(TRIM(email)) as normalized_email
    FROM users
    WHERE email IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
    HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
) d
ON LOWER(TRIM(u.email)) = d.normalized_email
ORDER BY d.normalized_email, u.id;

It's a normal aggregation query even on 2m rows, but an index would help. If your database allows it, you can put an index on the normalized value. (Postgresql, for example)

CREATE INDEX users_email_normalized_idx
ON users(LOWER(TRIM(email)));

And then for new inserts, you can enforce uniqueness if you don't want duplicates. For example (Postgresql):

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_unique_idx
ON users(LOWER(TRIM(email))::VARCHAR)
WHERE email IS NOT NULL;

Make sure you've cleaned or at least decided what to do about duplicates (the index create will fail as long as you have multiple of the same normalized email) before putting that in place.

Lets say you have a table 'users' with a column 'email'. You want to find out which emails are duplicated. You'll want to group by email, and only include groups that have multiple rows:

SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS duplicate_count FROM users WHERE email IS NOT NULL GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY duplicate_count DESC, email ; So this will give you a list of every duplicated email and how many times it is duplicated. If 'alex@example.com' is duplicated 3 times, you'll see something like: alex@example.com | 3

If you want duplicates to include emails that may have been capitalized and/or may have leading and trailing spaces... then you'll want to normalize those emails in your query: SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS normalized_email , COUNT(*) AS duplicate_count FROM users WHERE email IS NOT NULL GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email)) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY duplicate_count DESC ;

Now, how do you get the list of actual user records involved? Well, you can use a derived table: SELECT u.* FROM users AS u JOIN ( SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS normalized_email FROM users WHERE email IS NOT NULL GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email)) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ) AS d ON LOWER(TRIM(u.email)) = d.normalized_email ORDER BY d.normalized_email, u.id ;

This is still a regular 'agg' query - even though you have 2m rows. But perhaps you should have an index. If you can, set up an index on your normalized value. Say, if you're on Postgres. CREATE INDEX users_email_normalized_idx ON users (LOWER(TRIM(email)) ;

And to prevent duplicates in the future (if you don't want them). So for postgres, you might do: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_unique_idx ON users (LOWER(TRIM(email)) WHERE email IS NOT NULL ;

But you'll probably want to deal with your existing duplicates (or at least decide what to do about them) before adding this constraint - because you're not going to be able to create the index until you don't have duplicate normalized email addresses!

MEMORANDUM

TO: Maria Delgado, Chief Financial Officer FROM: James Okonkwo, Chief Information Security Officer DATE: March 14, 2025 RE: FY2026 Cybersecurity Budget Increase Request from $4.2M to $4.7M

PURPOSE
Requesting a 12% increase to our Cybersecurity Department budget for FY2026. This means increasing from $4.2M to $4.7M. This memo outlines rationale, allocation and impact.

RATIONALE
Request is based on three key factors:

1. Regulatory Environment. Increased monitoring and documentation needed due to audit preparation requirements (SOC 2 Type II) and new state privacy law that takes effect 01/01/2026. Estimated incremental compliance costs: $180k
2. Threat Landscape. We have seen 14 targeted phishing attempts this FY2025 (vs. 6 previous year). Also had two near ransomware misses in Q3 2025. Need to renew our SIEM licensing and 24/7 monitoring services contract with SentinelWatch. Both expire in August 2025. 9% premium required.
3. Business Growth. We have a new Denver office opening in October 2025. Our employee count will be at 850. We've increased our attack surface about 20% since our FY2024 budget was established.

ALLOCATION OF $500K INCREASE
• $220k to renew SIEM and increase monitoring coverage
• $165k to hire an additional security engineer (fully loaded 1 FTE)
• $75k to upgrade MFA and endpoint detection tools
• $40k to roll out employee security awareness training (across all offices)

ALTERNATIVES
Postponing SIEM renewal isn't an option. The coverage gap would breach cyber insurance policy terms. We'd have estimated $2M of uninsured liability. We looked at outsourcing for the new engineer. Managed services estimates 30% more expensive than hiring internally. (3 year period).

IMPACT
If approved, we expect to be audit compliant by Q2 FY2026. Mean time to detect threats will drop from 6 hours to <90 minutes. Zero Trust implementation will be complete by June 2026.

I'm happy to discuss further if you like. Can provide presentation to Finance Committee on April 22 if desired.

MEMORANDUM

To: All Employees
From: Dana Whitfield, VP of Human Resources
Date: November 14, 2024
Re: Enhancement to Parental Leave. Effective 1/1/2025

We are excited to announce that, based on a competitive benefits benchmarking analysis we ran this fall, we are increasing our paid parental leave from 8 to 16 weeks effective January 1, 2025!

Background
In Q3, HR ran a benchmark study of parental leave benefits among 12 peer companies in our industry (including our top 3 talent competitors). Median paid parental leave across these companies was 14 weeks. A few companies had recently increased their offerings to 16 weeks+ as well. Our current 8 weeks was below the bottom quartile. This was a cause for decline in offer acceptances in 23% of our recruiting exit surveys in the last 18 months.

Changes
Effective 1/1/2025, all eligible full-time employees that become a parent by birth, adoption or foster placement will be eligible for 16 weeks of paid parental leave (from the current 8 weeks). 
 Details:
? Leave needs to be taken within 12 months of child's arrival
? Available to all parents (regardless of gender or caregiver)
? Leave can be taken in 1 block or 2 (at manager's discretion)
? If you started leave on or after 10/1/2024, you can choose to extend your leave and use the new policy (reach out to HR)

No change: Employees are still protected for their jobs (FMLA + any applicable state) - we're actually now providing more.

No change: Short term disability benefits (8 weeks for birth mothers - through Lincoln Financial) are separate and run in parallel to the first weeks of parental leave.

No change: We still offer 4 weeks of paid caregiver leave for family medical emergencies.

Budget 
Estimated annual impact is $740K. Finance Committee approved this on 11/6 as part of our FY2025 benefits budget. We're hoping that this will help us also with reducing employee turnover (replacement cost was an average of 42% salary based on our 2023 analysis of replacement costs for employees that leave).

Please feel free to send any questions to hr@company.com. Or raise questions at December 3 all-hands meeting. We will publish a new policy document on the HR portal by 12/15.

MEMORANDUM

To: All Employees
From: Dana Whitfield, VP Human Resources
Date: November 14, 2024
Subject: Extension of Parental Leave Policy - Effective Jan 1st, 2025

We're excited to share that, after completing a competitive benefits benchmarking analysis this fall, we've decided to extend our paid parental leave from 8 weeks to 16 weeks effective January 1, 2025!

BACKGROUND
In Q3, we worked with HR to conduct a benchmarking analysis of parental leave benefits for our 12 peer companies within our industry, including our top 3 competitors from a talent perspective. The median paid parental leave for these peers is 14 weeks. Several firms have recently made the switch to 16+ weeks. Our current 8 weeks puts us in the lowest quartile and has been called out as a reason in 23% of declined offer acceptances over the past 18 months based on our recruiting exit surveys.

WHAT'S CHANGING
Starting January 1, 2025, any eligible full-time employees who have a child through birth, adoption, or foster placement will be eligible for 16 weeks of paid parental leave, an increase from 8 weeks. Specific details include:

- Must be used within 12 months of the child's arrival
- Any parent, regardless of gender or caretaking status, is eligible
- Can be used in one continuous block or up to two blocks, with manager approval
- For those who started their parental leave on or after Oct 1, 2024, you have the option to extend your leave based on the new policy. Just reach out to HR.

This policy continues to provide job protection as required under FMLA and relevant state laws (we're above and beyond!)

WHAT'S NOT CHANGING
Short-term disability (birth mothers, up to 8 weeks - through Lincoln Financial) is a separate benefit which runs concurrent with the first weeks of parental leave. We do not change our current 4 weeks paid caregiver leave for family medical emergencies.

BUDGET IMPACT
Estimated annual cost for this extension is $740K. This was approved by Finance Committee on Nov 6 as part of the FY2025 benefits budget. We do expect to see a reduction in turnover and the cost to replace employees, which was an average of 42% of salary based on our 2023 analysis, will help offset some of this cost.

If you have questions, please email hr@company.com or ask at our all hands meeting on Dec 3. We will post an updated policy to the HR portal by Dec 15.

TO: Executive Steering Committee
FROM: Finance & IT Strategy
RE: Summary of Cost/Benefit of ERP Cloud Migration
DATE: September 21, 2026

Recommendation: Approve $2.3M for migrating our on-prem SAP ECC 6.0 environment to a SaaS cloud based ERP (S/4HANA Cloud). Targeted go-live Q3 2027.

COST

$2.3M one-time investment made up of:
- Data migration/clean up ($620K)
- Rebuilding 14 system integrations (WMS, Salesforce etc) ($540K)
- Employee retraining ($310K) (180 users in Finance/Ops)
- Costs of parallel run for 4 months cutover ($450K)
- Contingency/PM overhead ($380K)
SaaS subscription cost is $890K per year. (vs current $1.15M/year for on-prem maintenance/hosting/support. = $260K annual run-rate savings)

PAYBACK

Net run-rate savings (above) plus no longer having to refresh $1.4M in servers (avoided capex in FY2027 since we are delaying). Plus est'd productivity savings of $310K per year from automated workflows. Payback in 3.1 years. 5-year NPV ~ $1.7M with 8% discount rate.

COMPLIANCE

* With SOC 2 Type II audit and GDPR (have a subsidiary in EU, Dublin). Need contractual guarantees for data residency from the vendor. Legal has confirmed proposed vendor meets the requirements with a data center in EU.

* With SOX need updated documentation for controls over changes to accommodate new release cadence model. With SaaS vendor our releases occur quarterly (out of our hands).

RISKS

1) Disruption to month end close during cutover (addressed with parallel period).
2) Resistance to change from some senior finance employees (addressed with employee retraining costs noted above).

NEXT

Looking for committee approval by 10/10/2026 to ensure we can lock in vendor pricing before their November rate increase.

The recommended action is to cease operations in the Centerville retail location at the end of the lease term on August 31, 2025. The Centerville store has persistently been a money-losing proposition, despite ongoing management focus, cost management, and sales enhancement initiatives. The operating losses at Centerville are detracting from the operations of other more profitable stores and are a drag on our investments in e-commerce, customer loyalty, and profitable markets.

Over the last 12 months, the Centerville store has produced about $1.2 million in sales while carrying about $1.45 million in operating costs for an estimated annual operating loss of $250,000. The store is showing average month-to-month sales decreases of about 8% over the previous year. Costs such as rent, personnel, utilities, and inventory holding costs are steadily rising. The traffic to the store is significantly less than what's needed to make this store work as currently sized.

By allowing the lease to expire at the end of the term, we would avoid the responsibility to renew the lease, cut fixed costs of operating, and sidestep spending about $150k on projected facility/merchandise capital expenditures. The store closure is estimated to yield a net increase in annual operating income of about $230k after allowing for one-time costs such as severance, product markdowns, relocation costs, and lease termination activities.

We recommend minimum 60-day notification to the Centerville store associates. Qualified personnel should be given the opportunity to transfer to other stores (Riverside and Northgate) where vacancies currently exist. Inventory should be phased out and transferred to neighboring stores and our online presence starting in June 2025, with a controlled clearance sale in July and August. Communicate with customers to reassure them of continued service via our online store and surrounding stores.

Formal notification to the landlord should be made by management no later than May 31, 2025. Employee discussions should be concluded by June 15, and the store should cease operations at the end of business on August 31, 2025. This is the prudent financial decision, operationally feasible and in line with our overall strategy of focusing on profitable venues and channels.

MEMORANDUM
 TO: 		All Department Heads and Regional Managers
 FROM:	Priya Nair, Director of Human Resources
 DATE:		April 14, 2025
 RE:			Remote Work Eligibility Changes. Results of March Staff Survey.

Purpose:
This memo highlights results of March 2025 (82% response rate) remote work survey (1240 respondents) and new eligibility changes to be in place starting June 2, 2025.

Key Survey Results:
-	74% of respondents agree on hybrid approach. Only 11% want 100% on-site.
-	87% of responses indicate that employees rate productivity on remote days the same or higher than on-site.
-	Least satisfaction levels from departments with set in-office policies (Facilities, Front Desk Services, Print Production).
-	63% respondents pointed out significant commute expenses. $340/month on average.

New Policy, effective June 2, 2025.
1.	Default to hybrid. Eligible employees can work remotely up to 3 days a week. (+1) As permitted by their manager.
2.	Fully Remote: Allow for fully remote work for all roles identified as location agnostic. (ex. 112 roles across IT, Finance and Marketing). Performance review on a quarterly basis.
3.	In-office required roles. Roles which need physical presence. Building security, Mail Room, Lab Techs (Portland/Denver site). These will be on-site. Provide commuter stipend of $75/month.

-	Managers to submit new hybrid agreements to HR. Deadline: May 16, 2025.
-	All employees need to update Remote Work Agreement in Workday. Deadline: May 30, 2025.
-	Remote employees within 50miles of Denver/Austin/Boston offices, need to come in on-site for team collaborative days at least once a month.

All remote arrangements are subject to state tax and labor laws where employees work. Employees wanting to move to out-of-state need 60 days advance notice. Subject to review with HR Legal.

MEMO

To: All Department Heads and Regional Managers From: Priya Nair, Director of Human Resources Date: April 14, 2025 Subject: Changes to Remote Work Eligibility (Update on March Staff Survey Results)

SUMMARY This memo provides an update on the March 2025 remote work survey results (82% response rate, 1,240 employees) and the updated eligibility criteria, which will take effect June 2, 2025.

March survey results key highlights:

• 74% of respondents support hybrid work environment while only 11% want everyone to be in office 100% of the time.
• 87% of respondents feel that their productivity (self-rating) was the same or better on remote work days.
• Departments with strict in-office requirements (e.g., Facilities, Front Desk services, Print production) are least satisfied. • 63% of employees consider commuting costs a major issue. Average monthly expense - $340.

The updated remote work policy will take effect June 2, 2025:

1) Hybrid work (maximum 3 days work from home/week from 2 day/week) - eligible employees can choose to work from home 3 days/week (up from 2 days) if approved by the manager.

2) Fully remote - roles classified as "location independent" (112 currently, in areas like IT, Finance and Marketing) can work 100% remote - (periodic performance check each quarter).

3) In-office roles required - roles like building security, mailroom, lab techs (Portland/Denver sites) that need in-person presence will be in-office. Commuting benefit provided - $75/month.

Implementation requirements:

• Managers to provide revised hybrid agreements to HR by May 16th, 2025 for each team. • All employees need to sign new remote work agreement in Workday by May 30th, 2025. • Remote workers within 50 miles of Denver, Austin and Boston offices need to be onsite at least once a month for team collaborative days.

Compliance:

Remote work is still subject to state tax and labor laws compliance in state/location where employees are working. When employees want to move to a different state, they need to give 60 days notice. HR Legal will need to review.

If you have any questions, please contact hr-policy@company.com or during the April 24th All Hands briefing.

The $340 million acquisition for TerraFusion Energy's geothermal assets (which includes 48MW Silver Basin project located near Winnemucca, Nevada and 32MW Coso Ridge expansion project located in Inyo County, California along with related exploration leases of about 41,000 acres of land in Nevada and eastern California) is justifiable as of September 21, 2026, assuming a pass for environmental, title and production diligence.

The price tag offers an estimated $4.25 million/MW per MW of installed capacity for 80 MW of operating and late-stage assets, which is a reasonable price for firm and renewable energy, especially if those assets qualify for clean energy federal tax credits and can deliver 24-hour capacity. Depending on the preliminary estimates, the portfolio would provide an annual revenue potential of around $58 million from an average contracted power price of $72/MWh before accounting for operating expenses and royalties.

The biggest risks center around depletion of resources, permitting hurdles, water usage constraints, and outstanding TerraFusion's obligations to counties and tribal interests. As such, the transaction should be structured as $290 million upfront payment upon closing with up to $50 million earn-out compensation based on milestones for production, permitting, and achieving commissioning for the Coso Ridge expansion by December 31, 2028.

The prospective buyer should press for an independent resource evaluation prior to closing as well as due diligence of 37 federal and state permits, land and mineral rights and five-year maintenance and capex plan. Additionally, management should ensure to have PPAs in place for at least 70% of the anticipated output and hold $35 million+ reserve for well remediation and unexpected drilling.

Under these circumstances the acquisition makes sense to bolster western U.S. renewable energy generation platform, providing reliable baseload capacity and supporting the 2030 emissions-reduction plan. Absent a pricing on milestones and confirmed resource analysis, the $340 million pricing tag should be dismissed.

As of September 21, 2026, subject to environmental, title and production due diligence, a $340m purchase price is warranted for the geothermal assets of TerraFusion Energy. The assets comprise 48MW Silver Basin (Winnemucca, NV) and 32MW Coso Ridge expansion (Inyo County, CA) and supporting exploration leases (approx. 41,000 acres) in Nevada and eastern California.

Based on estimated $4.25m/installed MW ($4.25m/MW) for 80MW (operating / late stage development), purchase price remains competitive for firm renewable energy, especially for potential access to clean energy federal tax credits and 24/7 capacity. Estimated revenues are approximately $58m annually (avg. contract power price ~$72/MWH), prior to operating expenses and royalties, per preliminary estimates.

Key risks include resource depletion, permitting challenges, water use limitations and TerraFusion's unresolved commitments to county and tribal entities. A deal structure should involve $290m at closing, with up to $50m earn-out consideration based on production milestones, permitting and Coso Ridge expansion commissioning (Dec. 31, 2028).

Prior to entering a deal, the acquiring company should insist on an independent resource assessment, 100% review of all 37 federal/state permits, land/mineral rights certainty, five-year maintenance/capital expenditures plan, a minimum of 70% coverage of power purchase agreements for expected output and a minimum $35m reserve for well remediation/unexpected drilling.

The acquisition would enhance the renewable generation portfolio in the western U.S., enhance dependable baseload capacity and contribute to the company's strategy for achieving emissions reduction targets in 2030. Absent earn-out pricing based on milestones and assured resource analysis, do not accept the $340m "headline" value.

paper_section_01_luna.text:
AlphaFold2, announced following 2020 CASP14 evaluation, published in Nature in 2021. AlphaFold2 brought a fundamental change to protein structure prediction. It exchanged information between multiple sequence alignment (MSA) and residue-pair representations multiple times with Evoformer using attention and outer-product operations. The information in these representations were transformed into 3D coordinates by a structure module utilizing invariant point attention (IPA). It leveraged sequence evolution, geometric reasoning and reused intermediate predictions to obtain median score of 92.4 GDT-TS in CASP14, including a median score of 87.0 on challenging free modeling targets. The IPA played a crucial role, as the attention is calculated on the learned 3D points but is invariant to global rotations and translations. [Jumper et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2).

Following AlphaFold2, there have been many new architectures that expand on the attention-centric approach. For example, RoseTTAFold from University of Washington, published in Science in 2021, introduced a network with three parallel tracks, handling 1D sequence/MSA features, 2D residue-pair features and 3D coordinates all at the same time. With the help of attention, graph transformer and SE(3)-equivariant layers, the representations could exchange information with each other. The end-to-end implementation took about 10 minutes to produce backbone coordinates using an RTX 2080 GPU for proteins smaller than 400 residues. [Baek et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abj8754).

At the same time, protein language models shifted the focus of structure prediction to the view that it is the result of sequence-scale representation learning. Meta's ESM-2 and ESMFold used the embeddings from the Transformer language model to predict structures of single sequence, avoiding heavy calculations on explicit MSA. It was published in Science in 2023. ESMFold powered the ESM Metagenomic Atlas with predictions for over 617 million proteins, yet the accuracy was generally lower than AlphaFold2. [Lin et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.ade2574).

AlphaFold3, published in Nature 2024. AlphaFold3 built on the work of protein folding prediction and ventured into the field of biomolecular interaction modeling. It replaced the AlphaFold2 structure module using IPA with a diffusion-based generative model, which can model proteins, nucleic acids, ligands, ions, and modified residues all together. This marks the progression of transformer-based protein prediction from MSA-conditioned geometric attention to multimodal foundation model that mixes language representations, equivariant geometry and diffusion coordinate generator.

AlphaFold2 which was released following CASP14 assessment in 2020 and published in Nature (2021) made a groundbreaking change in protein structure prediction. In AlphaFold2, Evoformer model was used to repeatedly update multiple sequence alignment (MSA) and residue pairs representations using attention and outer product calculation. Structure module (based on invariant point attention -IPA) was used to translate these representations into 3D coordinates. The effective combination of evolutionary and geometric information processing and recycled intermediate predictions enabled AlphaFold2 to reach 92.4 median GDT-TS in CASP14. Furthermore, median 87.0 was observed in challenging free modeling targets. IPA is of special importance where the attention is designed for learned 3D points and invariant to global rotations and translations. (Jumper et al., 2021 (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2))

Later, different architectures were designed to expand attention-based approach. One of them is RoseTTAfold that is developed at University of Washington and published in Science (2021). It is a three-track network to process 1D sequence/MSA information, 2D residue pairs and 3D coordinates in parallel. This architecture is able to keep information flow between these representations with attention, graph transformer and SE(3) equivariant layers. Furthermore, end-to-end implementation of the architecture produced backbone coordinates of proteins with length of <400 residues in ~10 min on an RTX 2080 GPU. (Baek et al., 2021 (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abj8754)) Protein language models also tried to understand that structure prediction is just a result of sequence scale representation learning. Protein structure prediction was made using language model (transformer) embeddings. Meta ESM2/ESMFold uses transformer language model embeddings to make structure prediction directly from sequences without computationally costly MSAs. Their model (published in Science (2023) and known as ESMFold) contributed to the emergence of the ESM Metagenomic Atlas (over 617M protein predictions) but in general accuracy is not as high as AlphaFold2's. (Lin et al., 2023 (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.ade2574))

AlphaFold3 (Nature (2024)) is another development of this trend from protein folding to biomolecular interaction modeling. This model has a generative architecture (based on diffusion) instead of AlphaFold2's structure module with IPA to simultaneously model proteins, nucleic acids, ligands, ions and modified residues. So, transformer-based protein modeling is moving from MSA-conditioned geometric attention to multi-modal foundation models with language representation, equivariant geometry and diffusion-based coordinate generation.

paper_section_03_glm.text:
Results

Incorporation of CsBr into the methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI 3 ) perovskite precursor solution resulted in statistically significant increase in the power conversion efficiency (PCE). 19.4% PCE of the best performing devices based on perovskites with 5 mol% CsBr vs. 18.1% PCE of control undoped devices resulted in 7.2% (1.3% absolute) relative yield increase. This effect was observed in 3 separate batches of device fabrication in March-May 2024 (best performing device PCE: 19.1-19.6% for CsBr doped vs. 17.8-18.3% for control).

Current density-voltage (J-V) characteristics under AM 1.5G (100 mW cm −2 ) indicated that open circuit voltage (V OC ) was the main contributor to the PCE increase (1.12 ± 0.02 V for doped vs. 1.06 ± 0.03 V for control devices, n = 24 for both types, p < 0.001, two-tail t-test), although slight increase in short circuit current density (J SC ) was observed (22.4 ± 0.6 → 22.9 ± 0.5 mA cm −2 ) while the fill factor remained statistically unchanged (FF = 0.74 ± 0.02 for both). Hysteresis index also decreased from 8.3% to 4.1% after addition of CsBr, which is in line with decrease in ion migration.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) on doped perovskite films showed that the (110) peak shifted by 0.14 o toward larger 2θ values while the PbI 2 peak (at 12.7 o ) disappeared. This suggests that part of the A site was replaced with Cs + ion and phase purity increased. Scanning electron microscopy images revealed larger grains (mean size 412 ± 95 vs. 287 ± 78 nm for control), which correlated with the decrease in trap state density determined by space charge limited current analysis (1.8 • 10 16 → 1.1 • 10 16 cm −3 ).

Device stability measurements under continuous illumination at 65 °C showed that the doped devices kept 88% of initial PCE after 500 h while control devices maintained 74% of initial PCE. Higher CsBr concentrations (10 and 15 mol% tested) resulted in phase segregation and decrease in performance (PCE 17.2% and 15.9% respectively) indicating that 5 mol% CsBr was optimal within the investigated composition space.

Results
The introduction of cesium bromide (CsBr) into the methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI3) precursor perovskite solution was shown to significantly increase the power conversion efficiency (PCE). In particular, the 5 mol% CsBr-doped perovskite had a champion PCE value of 19.4% compared to 18.1% for the control, undoped device. This yields a 7.2% (1.3% abs.) relative yield increase. This effect was confirmed in 3 different batches made in March–May 2024 (champion PCE in CsBr doped devices is 19.1–19.6% vs. 17.8–18.3% in the control).

The J-V characterization under AM 1.5G (100 mW cm −2) indicated that the increase in efficiency was mostly due to an increase in open circuit voltage (Voc). Doped devices had 1.12 ± 0.02 V vs. 1.06 ± 0.03 V in the control (n = 24 each, p < 0.001, two-tailed t-test). Short-circuit current density (JSC) was slightly higher at 22.9 ± 0.5 mA cm −2 compared to 22.4 ± 0.6 mA cm −2. Fill factor was not significantly different (FF = 0.74 ± 0.02 for both groups). The hysteresis indices were lower in the CsBr-doped devices (8.3% vs. 4.1%), indicating a decrease in ion migration.

The X-ray diffraction (XRD) of the CsBr-doped films showed a shift of (110) reflection by 0.14° to larger 2θ values and disappearance of the PbI2 peak at 12.7°, suggesting that part of the Cs + ions are incorporated into the A-site and that the phase purity is increased. From SEM analysis the grain size is larger (412 ± 95 nm vs. 287 ± 78 nm for the control) which is correlated to the lower trap state density (1.8 × 10 16 to 1.1 × 10 16 cm −3) as determined from the space-charge-limited current analysis.

In constant illumination and at 65 • C, the CsBr-doped devices maintained 88% of their initial PCE after 500 h, while the control devices kept 74%. When using CsBr concentrations higher than 5 mol% (10 and 15 mol% as tested), phase separation occurs and the device performance decreases (PCE = 17.2% and 15.9%, respectively). Therefore, 5 mol% CsBr is optimal in the tested composition range.

paper_section_05_sonnet.text:
Gradient boosting for 90-day hospital readmission risk prediction from longitudinal electronic health record data from the MIMIC-IV

Background: 90-day unplanned readmission post-discharge is a high cost and clinically important outcome but most risk prediction models focus on the 30-day readmission outcomes that CMS requires reporting, and there is little focus on a longer-term time horizon.

Methods: From MIMIC-IV v2.2 database (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA) we obtained 51,238 adult inpatient admissions between 2008 and 2019, excluding in-hospital deaths and hospice discharges for 46,904 index admissions for the eligible population. We defined the outcome of 90-day readmission as any subsequent inpatient encounter within 90 days post-discharge (positive rate: 21.4%, n=10,038). We created 187 features including demographic information, Elixhauser comorbidity indexes, admission severity (SOFA, SAPS-II), laboratory trends over the last 48 hours of the inpatient stay, number of medications at the time of discharge, length of stay, and prior utilization (ED visit/admissions in the last 12 months). We divided the patients according to unique subject ID (70/15/15 training/validation/test) to avoid inter-visit leakage. XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost classifiers were trained and compared. We performed hyperparameter optimization using 5-fold cross-validated Bayesian optimization (100 trials, Optuna) on the training set with early stopping at validation AUROC.

Results: LightGBM showed the best performance on held-out data (AUROC=0.762, 95% CI:0.748-0.776; AUPRC=0.451; Brier score=0.142). It performed better than logistic regression (AUROC=0.681), and slightly better than XGBoost (AUROC=0.754) and CatBoost (AUROC=0.758). From SHAP analysis, the main predictors were the number of prior 12-month admissions, hemoglobin at discharge, Elixhauser comorbidity score, and discharge destination (skilled nursing vs. home). The model was well calibrated with respect to deciles of risk (Hosmer-Lemeshow p=0.34). For a threshold that would identify the top 20% of predicted risk, the model sensitivity (proportion of true readmissions identified) was 58.3% and the positive predictive value was 47.1%.

Conclusions: We found that gradient boosting models from routine data elements in MIMIC-IV have clinically relevant discrimination for 90-day readmission risk, which may be useful in expanding discharge planning interventions to go beyond the traditional focus on the 30-day period. Need external validation in non-ICU weighted cohorts.

Predicting 90-day hospital readmissions with gradient boosting models from longitudinal data of MIMIC-IV electronic health records

Background: 90-day hospital readmission following discharge remains an important and costly outcome. However, many models focus on the 30-day readmission rate which is required by CMS reporting.

Methods: 51,238 adult inpatient admissions (2008-2019) from MIMIC-IV v2.2 database (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA) were identified after removing in-hospital mortality and hospice discharge. 46,904 qualified as index admissions. 90-day readmission was identified as any inpatient visit within 90-days from index discharge date (positive rate: 21.4% (n=10,038). A total of 187 features were extracted including demographic information, Elixhauser comorbidity indices, admission acuity (SOFA, SAPS-II), lab trends within the last 48 h of stay, number of discharge medications, length of stay, and use (ED visit, admission) in the last 12-months. Patients were separated by unique subject-ID (train/validation/test split at 70%/15%/15%) to avoid encounter leakage. XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost classifiers were developed and compared. Hyperparameters were optimized using 5-fold CV Bayesian optimization (n=100 trials, Optuna) on training data set with early stopping on validation AUROC.

Results: LightGBM model showed the highest test (AUROC: 0.762, 95% CI: 0.748 - 0.776; AUPRC: 0.451; Brier score: 0.142) performance compared to logistic regression baseline (AUROC: 0.681). The LightGBM model performed slightly better than XGBoost (AUROC: 0.754) and CatBoost (AUROC: 0.758). Key predictors of readmission included 12-month number of admission, discharge hemoglobin, Elixhauser comorbidity score, and discharge disposition (skilled nursing vs home) (per SHAP). The model showed good calibration across risk deciles (Hosmer-Lemeshow p=0.34). When model is set to identify top 20% of risk, it had a sensitivity of 58.3% in identifying true readmissions and a positive predictive value of 47.1%.

Conclusions: Gradient boosting classifiers leveraging the readily available data within MIMIC-IV for 90-day readmission risk discrimination provide clinically meaningful results. Thus, this approach can be used to expand discharge intervention scope to beyond the traditional 30-day readmission period (not validated externally on non-ICU-weighted populations).
