We conducted a field experiment in Kenya's Makueni and Kitui counties from October 2023 to August 2024 with 1,150 smallholder vegetable farmers. Households were sampled from village-level agricultural registers and pre-screened to ensure respondents: (1) farmed between 0.1 and 2.0 ha; (2) primarily rain-fed or manually irrigated; (3) did not currently use drip irrigation. Baseline surveys were completed, and participants were stratified by county and baseline irrigated area. They were randomized into information-only (n=383), information+50% voucher for drip-irrigation kit (n=384), or information+75% voucher (n=383).

All treatment households participated in a 2-hour demonstration led by local agricultural extension agents (trained by us) in November 2023. Demonstrations focused on how to install and maintain, potential water savings and crop-specific application rates. A 0.1 ha demonstration plot was set up. Vouchers could be redeemed from participating agro-dealers in Makueni and Kitui until February 29, 2024. Drip irrigation kits comprised 500 L storage tank, low-pressure filter, 100 m lateral tubing, connectors. Estimated that it could irrigate 0.1 ha. Information-only group was given the same technical information. There was no price subsidy.

Surveys were conducted in-person (enumerators blinded to treatment). Surveys were carried out at baseline. Four months after voucher expiration. At the end of the 2024 main growing season. Adoption (the main outcome) was defined as installation and use of a drip irrigation system on at least 0.05 ha in the 30 days prior to the endline survey. Secondary outcomes included area farmed, irrigation frequency, input expenses, vegetable yields, farm revenue, water use, perceived labor. For crop production: farmer records. Randomly selected crop-cutting plots. Intention-to-treat effects estimated using OLS. Included county fixed effects and pre-specified baseline variables as covariates. Standard errors clustered at the village level.

In a field experiment in Kenya between October 2023 and August 2024, 1,150 vegetable-growing smallholder farmers in Makueni and Kitui counties were sampled from village-level agricultural registers. Farmers were screened to ensure they (1) farmed between 0.1 and 2.0 hectares, (2) primarily practiced rain-fed or manual irrigation farming methods, and (3) had not yet adopted drip irrigation. Baseline data were collected from these farmers, and farmers were stratified on county of residence and initial irrigated area. Finally, farmers were randomly divided into three groups: a control group receiving only information (n = 383), a treatment group receiving information and a 50% voucher for a drip irrigation kit (n = 384), and a second treatment group receiving information and a 75% voucher for the drip kit (n = 383).

In November 2023, all treated farmers were invited to a two-hour demonstration on drip-irrigation installation, operation, potential water savings, and crop-specific drip rates held by trained local agricultural extension agents. The 0.1 hectare demonstration field showcased installation and operation. Until February 29, 2024, the vouchers could be redeemed at the participating agro-dealers in Makueni and Kitui. The drip kit consisted of a 500 liter storage tank, low pressure filter, 100 meters lateral tubing, connectors, and would, by estimation, cover a 0.1 hectare plot. While the treated farmers received a discount on the drip kits, the control group only received the technical information.

Baseline and post-intervention data were collected by trained enumerators who were unaware of the farmers' treatment status. Data were gathered in person for the baseline, four months after the vouchers' expiration date, and at the end of the 2024 main growing season. The main outcome variable is adoption, measured as the installation and use of a drip irrigation system on at least 0.05 hectares in the 30 days prior to the endline survey. Additional outcome variables include crop acreage, irrigation frequency, input costs, vegetable yield, farm income, water use, and self-reported labor. For agricultural production, we use farmer records and randomly sampled crop cutting plots. We use ordinary least squares estimation to measure intention to treat effects, including fixed effects for county and a set of pre-specified baseline controls. Standard errors are clustered by village.

paper_section_09_glm.text:
Discussion
 As anticipated, the 8 weeks HFD (60% kcal from fat) resulted in marked and highly reproducible alterations of the murine cecal microbiota at the genus level. As previous studies have shown (Bäckhed et al., 2004; Turnbaugh et al., 2006), the HFD resulted in strong changes in the murine cecal microbiota (C57BL/6J) (HFD n = 12; control (chow) n = 11). We found the most significant changes to be a 14.3-fold increase in *Bilophila* (log2 fold change 3.84; adjusted q-value = 0.002 -DESeq2 and Benjamini Hochberg correction). *Bilophila* has been described to be bile tolerant and mechanistic correlates are known to exist with the rise in tauroconjugated bile acids in response to fat feeding. Our data confirm the hypothesis that *Bilophila*-induced sulfide production affects the intestinal barrier.
 In contrast, we found a strong reduction of *Akkermansia*, a genus known to be involved in mucin degradation with documented beneficial effects on metabolic health in both mouse and man (log2FC = -2.61; q = 0.008). The causative or resulting character of the *Akkermansia* reduction in the context of HFD induced metabolic endotoxemia is still to be determined. We found that the reduction of *Akkermansia* occurred ~ 2 weeks before a rise in fasting glucose became detectable which suggests a directionality in this change. However, the experimental setup prevents us from drawing conclusions about causality.
 We must be careful when interpreting some results. First, the reduction of *Lactobacillus* (log2FC = -1.78; q = 0.03) was strongly influenced by only 3 individuals in our analysis. When removing these individuals from the analysis the change was not significant (q = 0.11) (sensitivity analysis). Second, the apparently increased abundance of *Clostridium* XIVa (log2FC = 1.92; q = 0.048) showed borderline significance and could be an effect of normalization of the data and thus could be a consequence of a compositional change (a known drawback of relative counts) -we partially overcame this by using ANCOM-BC for additional confirmation.
 HFD animals tended to show a decrease of alpha diversity (mean Shannon index: 3.12 HFD vs. 3.58 control; Wilcoxon p-value = 0.009). Also, beta diversity was different between the groups (PCo1 PERMANOVA R² = 0.19; p = 0.001), which suggests a significant re-structuring of the microbiota due to dietary perturbation. We are currently interested in whether and how these changes revert in response to the normalized diet. Also, which taxa correlate with insulin sensitivity recovery. This is the subject of an ongoing study in our laboratory.

Discussion.
In agreement with previous studies (Bäckhed et al., 2004; Turnbaugh et al., 2006), we find that exposure to a high fat diet (HFD) for 8 weeks (60% kcal fat) leads to substantial, and largely reproducible changes in murine cecal microbiota at genus level. Here we add quantitative detail in the form of effect size and individual variation. In C57BL/6J (HFD: n = 12 vs chow fed controls: n = 11) the strongest effect seems to be a 14.3x increase of *Bilophila* (log2 fold change = 3.84, adjusted q = 0.002, DESeq2 and Benjamini-Hochberg). This organisms has the organismal physiology (bile tolerance) to be mechanistically linked to the increase of tauro-conjugated bile acid (BA) that follows dietary fat intake. In agreement with proposed links between sulfide production by *Bilophila* and gut barrier dysfunction.

On the other hand, we also find a striking reduction of *Akkermansia* (log2FC = -2.61, q = 0.008) a mucin-degrading genus with a clear track record of metabolic beneficial effects in both rodents and humans. It is not clear if the reduction of *Akkermansia* is a cause or consequence of metabolic endotoxemia induced by HFD. Our data suggests that the reduction of *Akkermansia* preceded the detectable increase of fasting glucose by ~2 weeks suggesting a causal relationship, but we are unable to determine causation with the current study.

Care needs to be taken with two findings:
1)The reduction in *Lactobacillus* (log2FC = -1.78, q = 0.03) seemed to be caused by three individual animals, removal of these animals showed a not significant effect (q = 0.11 in a sensitivity analysis).
2)Apparent increase in *Clostridium* XIVa (log2FC = 1.92, q = 0.048) was borderline significant and may be an artifact of compositional normalization rather than an actual abundance change (an issue with relative abundance data which we tried to address somewhat with ANCOM-BC as confirmatory approach).

There is a small reduction in alpha diversity (mean Shannon 3.12 vs 3.58, p = 0.009 Wilcoxon) and a significant separation of beta diversity along PCo1 (PERMANOVA, R2 = 0.19, p = 0.001) suggesting that the diet perturbation has indeed altered community structure beyond single genera. Whether these effects are reversible once the diet is normalized and what genera are associated with restoration of insulin sensitivity is the subject of ongoing efforts in our lab.

paper_section_11_sonnet.text:
From a sensitivity analysis procedure, heterogeneous treatment effects have become one of the key topics in labor economics. Bayesian methods have excelled at inference in sparse high dimensional regimes that are common in policy evaluation studies. When classical methods are unable to express meaningful uncertainties around treatment effects estimated in narrow subgroup, Bayesian hierarchical models can partially pool information across groups and thus shrink estimates in noisy subgroups to more robust population averages. This approach has origins in Rubin (1981) work on parallel experiments and has seen broad empiricism in labor economics in evaluating job training programs (e.g. reanalysis of National Supported Work Demonstration data from the seminal LaLonde (1986) paper).

In the last decade Bayesian approaches have become more relevant because of (1) application of Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (Chipman, George, McCulloch (2010) in causal analysis (e.g. in Hill (2011) Bayesian Causal Forest), which allow for flexible nonparametric estimation of conditional average treatment effects with full posterior uncertainty estimates, and (2) a stream of empirical papers that use large scale administrative data (e.g. Angrist, Pallais etc. work on job search assistance programs) or work with Danish/German social insurance data (more than one million workers) that showed enormous gains of Bayesian shrinkage over unpooled subgroup estimates when treatment effects depend on hundreds of strata (e.g. age, education, local labor market characteristics).

The literature has also extensively explored Bayesian instrumental variables and regression discontinuity designs (where issues of weak instruments often arise, e.g. minimum wages, extension of unemployment insurance). See for example Bayesian approach to welfare-to-work experiments by Kline and Tartari (2016), or meta analysis of microcredit trials by Meager (2019) showing how hierarchical priors can help bridge sometimes conflicting results at different sites.

We will provide an overview of this literature, assess relative performance of different approaches in simulated labor market data (calibrated to the 2019 Current Population Survey) and offer advice on the choice of BART, Gaussian Process, shrinkage prior estimators for applied researchers.

Heterogeneous treatment effect estimation has become an important goal (from being a robustness exercise) in labor economics, and Bayesian approaches have proven particularly appealing in the sparse high-dimensional settings common to policy evaluation. In contrast to classical approaches for which it can be difficult to provide meaningful estimates of uncertainty for treatment effects within small subgroups, Bayesian hierarchical models provide (through partial pooling) the ability to borrow information across subgroups, which helps shrink less stable treatment estimates from subgroups towards more stable treatment estimates at the population level. This concept emerged from Rubin's (1981) parallel experiments literature, and empirical applications in labor economics gained in popularity for their use in estimating treatment effects of job training programs (especially re-analyses of National Supported Work Demonstration data initially studied by LaLonde (1986)).

In the last decade, there have been two major sources of increased popularity for Bayesian approaches. First, the development of Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (Chipman, George, and McCulloch 2010) for causal inference, as demonstrated by the use of Bayesian Causal Forests (Hill 2011) facilitates nonparametric flexible estimation of conditional average treatment effects while maintaining full quantification of posterior uncertainty. Second, applied research that often uses large administrative datasets (e.g., Angrist, Pallais et al. for job search assistance programs; also using Danish and German social insurance data that include more than 1 million workers) has shown that Bayesian shrinkage vastly improves estimation of treatment effects across hundreds of subgroups (e.g., grouped by age, education, and local labor market conditions) relative to the use of un-pooled subgroup estimates.

Bayesian approaches have also been applied to instrumental variables and regression discontinuity approaches, as another stream of literature has focused on Bayesian approaches for these settings (e.g., to help with weak instruments in minimum wage effects and unemployment insurance extensions). For example, Kline and Tartari's (2016) Bayesian analysis of welfare to work experiments and Meager's (2019) meta-analysis of micro-credit trials show how use of hierarchical priors help provide solutions for apparent conflicts in findings across locations.

This paper will survey these methodological approaches, discuss their relative performance on simulated labor market data (following parameters of the 2019 Current Population Survey), and offer some advice to applied researchers on how to select among BART, Gaussian processes, and shrinkage prior estimators.

paper_section_13_luna.text:
A preferred response to point-light walker stimuli was consistently demonstrated by 64 healthy infants (32 female, 32 male; 5-7 months; M = 6.1 months; SD = 0.7) examined from March - August 2024 in the University of Washington Infant Learning and Development Laboratory in Seattle. Each infant was presented with 24 trials comprised of an upright or inverted point-light walker stimulus or a phase-scrambled motion control and a visually matched set of stationary dots. Only trials where valid gaze was obtained for 50% of the 2s display period were retained (91.8% valid trials).

Infants showed a significantly greater preference for the upright walker display than the matched control stimulus in their total amount of looking time (M = 61.7%; 95% CI [59.2, 64.2]), t(63) = 5.84, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.73. The upright walker stimulus was also preferentially first-fixated, 68% of trials, a significant preference above chance, χ 2(1) = 13.76, p < .001. By contrast, looking toward the inverted walker (M = 51.9%) or scrambled displays (M = 49.8%) was not significantly above chance, t(63) = 1.21, p = .23; t(63) = -0.18, p = .86, respectively. A linear mixed-effects model with factors including infant age, sex, trial type, and trial number, showed a significant main effect for display type, F(2, 126) = 12.47, p < .001. Pairwise comparisons showed that looking was significantly greater for the upright walkers stimulus than the inverted walker (mean difference = 9.8% points, p = .002) and scrambled stimuli (mean difference = 11.9% points, p < .001). There were no significant effects of infant age or sex on the preference.

These results show that infants at 5-7 months of age prefer the coherent kinematic display of human biological motion to local dot movement and global stimulus energy.

Consistent preference for point-light walker displays in 64 healthy 5-7 month old infants from University of Washington Infant Learning and Development Laboratory in Seattle March-August 2024. Thirty-two females and 32 males. Age: M = 6.1, SD = 0.7 months. Eye tracking data showed consistent preferences for upright point-light walker displays (24 trials; upright point-light walker vs. inverted walker vs. scrambled phase motion control with visually matched dot static array). Only trials that had valid eye tracking data for 50% or more of the 2 s trial presentation were included (91.8% valid samples).

Total time looking to upright walker displays (M = 61.7%, 95% CI [59.2,64.2]) was higher than the total time looking to the corresponding control stimuli, t(63) = 5.84, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.73. There was also a significant preference in first fixation to upright walker (68% of trials, significantly greater than chance), χ²(1) = 13.76, p < .001. However, there was no consistent above chance looking to the inverted walker displays (M = 51.9%), t(63) = 1.21, p = .23, or scrambled displays (M = 49.8%), t(63) = -0.18, p = .86. Linear mixed-effects model with infant age, sex, trial type and trial number; the type of display was significant, F(2,126) = 12.47, p < .001. Pairwise comparisons showed that upright walkers attracted more looking than both inverted walkers (mean difference = 9.8 percentage points, p = .002) and scrambled (mean difference = 11.9 percentage points, p < .001). The preference for upright walkers was not significantly moderated by infant age or sex. These results suggest that at 5-7 months old, infants appear to be sensitive to the coherent kinematic pattern of human biological motion rather than just dot motion and stimulus energy.

Abstract Mindfulness training has been suggested to improve working memory capacity (WMC) as a cost-effective strategy, but individual studies show inconsistent findings with different effect sizes. This meta-analysis aims to estimate the net effect of mindfulness-based training on WMC and to examine the moderators of training effectiveness. We conducted a literature search across databases (PsycINFO, PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus) between January 2000 and March 2024 and selected 38 studies (k = 41 independent samples, N = 3,247 participants) that compared mindfulness training against active/no intervention control groups and measured WMC through behavioral tasks (e.g., complex span tasks, n-back tasks, operation span task, etc.). The random-effects model showed a small-to-moderate net effect size (Hedges's g = 0.38, 95% CI = [0.24, 0.52]; p < .001) with significant effect heterogeneity (Q = 96.4; I 2 = 58.6%). Moderation analysis showed that longer training (≥ 8 weeks vs. < 8 weeks; β = 0.21; p = .012), face-to-face training compared to app training (g = 0.46 vs. 0.22; p = .031) and populations with high pre-existing stress (e.g., students at exam time, military personnel before deployment) had larger effects. The effects did not significantly vary across age groups, meditation techniques (focused attention vs. open monitoring) or publication years. Most studies were rated as low risk of bias (12 studies), some concerns (21 studies) or high risk (5 studies) by RoB 2 tool. Egger's regression test showed a possible presence of small-study effect (p = .048) and trim-and-fill analysis indicated a slightly smaller corrected effect size (g = 0.31). The robustness of the overall effect was checked by sensitivity analyses controlling for outliers and type of control groups. Our results suggest that structured mindfulness training could lead to modest, reliable enhancement of working memory capacity, especially when the training is at least eight weeks long and face-to-face under a live instructor. However, the findings need to be considered with caution because of effect heterogeneity and possible publication bias. We discuss the implications for cognitive training research and make recommendations for future randomized studies including preregistration, sufficient active control conditions and large sample size.

Keywords: mindfulness, working memory, meta-analysis, cognitive training, intervention

Abstract
Mindfulness training has been considered as a low-cost method of improving working memory capacity (WMC) but there are conflicting and mixed effects of different magnitude in the individual studies. To determine the overall effect of mindfulness-based interventions on WMC and to find moderators of mindfulness training effectiveness, we conducted a meta-analysis. We identified 38 eligible studies (k = 41 independent samples, N = 3247 participants) that compared mindfulness training to active or no intervention control groups published in January 2000 to March 2024 in PsycINFO, PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and that evaluated WMC using behavioral methods (e.g., complex span tasks, n-back, Operation Span task). The overall effect size was small to moderate using random-effects models (Hedges' g = 0.38, 95% CI [0.24, 0.52], p < .001) with significant heterogeneity (Q = 96.4, I 2 = 58.6%). The moderator analyses showed a greater effect with longer interventions (≥ 8 weeks versus < 8 weeks, β = 0.21, p = .012), instructor-led mindfulness interventions versus app-based (g = 0.46 vs. 0.22, p = .031), and for samples with higher initial stress levels (e.g., students during examination period, military personnel before deployment). The effects did not differ based on age, type of meditation (focused attention vs. open monitoring), or publication year. The risk-of-bias analysis using RoB 2 revealed that 12 studies were low risk of bias, 21 studies were some concerns, and 5 studies were high risk of bias. Egger's regression test showed that there may be small study effects (p = .048). Trim and fill analysis provided a lower corrected estimate of g = 0.31. Sensitivity analysis showed that the overall effect was robust to outliers and control type. Thus, mindfulness training in a structured way with longer duration (e.g., ≥ 8 weeks) and using live instructors might provide modest and consistent improvements to working memory capacity. However, there is heterogeneity and likely publication bias to consider. We discuss the implications of our results for cognitive training research and provide recommendations for future randomized studies (e.g., preregistration, appropriate active control, larger sample size).

Keywords
mindfulness, working memory, meta-analysis, cognitive training, intervention

Methods
We exploit the 2014 minimum wage ordinance in Seattle to examine effects on employment using a difference-in-differences strategy based on Seattle versus a synthetic control formed from adjacent ZIP codes in King County and similar labor markets outside the Seattle-Tacoma-Bellevue metropolitan statistical area in Washington State. The Seattle City Council approved the ordinance (June 2, 2014), which incrementally increased the minimum wage from the state minimum of $9.47/hour starting April 1, 2015 to $11.00/hour (large employers 500+ employees) up to $15.00/hour (January 1, 2017 for large employers with no medical benefits; January 1, 2019 for small employers).

We use data from Washington State Employment Security Department's quarterly Unemployment Insurance (UI) wage records (2005Q1-2018Q4) for hourly workers in sectors with the largest number of jobs subject to the minimum wage: food service (NAICS 722) and retail trade (NAICS 44-45). We create a balanced panel of 2,847 establishments with uninterrupted observations through the sample period, with comparison establishments identified using propensity score weighting (pre-period 2005Q1-2014Q2 trends in hours, headcount and average hourly wage).

The base specification is: Yit βSeattlei× Postt αi γt Xitδ εit where Yit is the log employment or log hours for establishment i in quarter t. Seattlei is an indicator for treatment establishments, Postt is an indicator for post-April 2015, αi and γt are establishment and quarter fixed effects, Xit is establishment size and single-site indicators. We cluster standard errors by ZIP code (94 clusters). We test for parallel trends using event study coefficients, where coefficients for all quarters from 2013Q1 to 2018Q4 (with 2015Q1 omitted as the reference period) are separately estimated for each quarter. We also estimate separately by wage tier bins ($9.47 to $11, $11 to $13, > $13) for differential bite by wage.

Methods
We use a difference-in-differences research design that compares Seattle to a synthetic control comprised of neighboring zip codes in King County and similar labor markets in Washington State outside of the Seattle-Tacoma-Bellevue metropolitan statistical area to estimate the employment impacts of Seattle's 2014 minimum wage law. On June 2, 2014, the Seattle City Council approved an ordinance that increases the minimum wage in stages, starting April 1, 2015. The minimum wage rises from the state-level floor of $9.47 to $11.00 for large firms (500+ employees) with further increases to $15.00 on January 1, 2017 (for large firms without medical benefits) and January 1, 2019 (for small firms).

We use the Washington State Employment Security Department's quarterly Unemployment Insurance (UI) wage data for 2005Q1-2018Q4 for hourly workers in food service (NAICS 722) and retail trade (NAICS 44-45) where we see the largest share of min-wage-bound jobs. We create a balanced panel of 2,847 establishments that have data throughout the sample period. We match the panel to other establishments using propensity score weights that match on pre-treatment (2005Q1-2014Q2) trends in hours, headcount, and average hourly wages.

The base specification is as follows:
Y_it = beta (Seattle_i * Post_t) + alpha_i + gamma_t + X_it*delta + epsilon_it

Where, Y_it is the log employment or hours for establishment i in quarter t, Seattle_i is a dummy variable for treated establishments, Post_t is a dummy variable for quarters after April 2015, alpha_i and gamma_t are establishment and quarter fixed effects, X_it are controls for establishment size and single site status. We cluster our standard errors by zip code (94 clusters). We examine the validity of parallel trends by estimating the event study coefficients individually for each quarter (2013Q1 to 2018Q4) relative to the omitted period 2015Q1. We present estimates by wage tier bins ($9.47-$11, $11-$13, greater than $13) to examine heterogeneity in the bite of the change to the wage distribution.

Glass transition in PMMA/PVDF blends is unusual, since segmental mobility is significantly different between PMMA which in most cases shows the \(T_g\) in the region of 105–125 °C, and PVDF which shows \(T_g\) near −50 °C. In spite of the difference, it is frequently observed in the differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) a single \(T_g\) (composition-dependent) instead of two independent glass transitions. This means that there is an extensive molecular-level mixing in blends which is mainly driven by carbonyl PMMA–H-bearing PVDF interactions. In initial calorimetric study, Roerdink et al. [1978] observed compatibility in wide compositional ranges for blends made of isotactic, atactic and syndiotactic PMMA/PVDF. The \(T_g\) values obtained were not exhibiting universal linear interpolation, instead they have been fitted according to the Gordon–Taylor equation for composition- and tacticity-dependent \(k\) values 2.38, 1.72, 1.39 for isotactic, atactic and syndiotactic PMMA, respectively ([Roerdink et al., 1978](https://doi.org/10.1016/0032-3861(78)90034-4)).

The anomaly becomes more significant for high PVDF contents when crystallization and nano-scale concentration fluctuations could lead to transition broadening or shift. As for the specific weak interactions Huang and Zhang [2004] found some evidence of them e.g. shift of the carbonyl stretching peak in IR spectra, however also increasing heterogeneity and opacity with rising PVDF content. Therefore it cannot be assumed that single transition observed by DSC means full thermodynamic homogeneity. Dielectric relaxation study of 4:1 and 3:2 PMMA/PVDF blends in 2020 showed higher strength and conductivity of relaxation which is an indication of nano-scale heterogeneity in blends ([Gonçalves et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1080/00222348.2020.1847393)). Anomalous \(T_g\) response arises due to competition of specific interchain interactions, free-volume content as a function of composition, PVDF crystallinity and history of preparation. Integrated analysis combining DSC with spectroscopy, dynamic mechanical and dielectric studies is needed to properly interpret the results, instead of treating \(T_g\) as a parameter for the binary miscibility.

PMMA/PVDF blends show anomalous glass transition behavior. The glass transition of PMMA usually occurs at 105-125 °C, while for PVDF it's around −50 °C, reflecting the huge difference in their segmental dynamics. Nevertheless, DSC frequently shows only a single, composition-dependent transition, rather than the expected double glass transition. This point towards significant mixing at the molecular level, driven by the specific interactions of carbonyls of PMMA and the H-segments of PVDF. In a pioneer calorimetric study, Roerdink et al. (1978) demonstrated the compatibility of isotactic, atactic and syndiotactic PMMA/PVDF blends over wide ranges of composition. But the obtained Tg's did not follow a universal linear interpolation, but were more consistent with the Gordon-Taylor equation, with the k depending on composition and tacticity, being 2.38, 1.72 and 1.39 for i-, a- and s-PMMA, respectively [Roerdink et al., 1978] (https://doi.org/10.1016/0032-3861(78)90034-4).

The apparent anomaly is more severe when the PVDF content is high, due to crystallization and nanoscale compositional fluctuations affecting the broadening or displacement of the transition. While Huang and Zhang (2004) found indications of weak specific interactions (including a shift of carbonyl stretching in the IR spectrum), they also observed increasing heterogeneity and opacity with higher PVDF content. So, a single DSC transition does not necessarily mean complete thermodynamic homogeneity. For instance, dielectric relaxation measurements in 4:1 and 3:2 PMMA/PVDF in 2020 have shown higher relaxation intensity and conductivity, which can be taken as a sign of nanoscale compositional heterogeneity [Gonçalves et al., 2020] (https://doi.org/10.1080/00222348.2020.1847393). The anomalous behavior of Tg is thus determined by the interplay between interchain specific interactions, composition-dependent free volume, crystallization of PVDF, and processing conditions. A proper understanding of this behavior needs more than DSC, as combined use of spectroscopic, dynamic mechanical and dielectric properties is necessary, and the use of Tg as a single criterion of binary miscibility may be inadequate.

Introduction Chemotherapy dose determination stands as a critical yet sub-optimally managed treatment decision in oncology. The current standard of care dosing of cytotoxic agents (e.g., 5-fluorouracil, carboplatin, doxorubicin) was largely defined by population dose-finding studies in the 1980s-1990s, typically using fixed dose/BSA normalized levels (with protocol dictated dose de-escalation for toxicity). This paradigm of "one-size fits all" disregards the large range of inter-and intra-patient pharmacokinetic variability that often (more than 10x range in clearance) defines cytotoxic chemotherapy. The effect of suboptimal dosing on clinical outcomes is well established; underdosing leads to suboptimal tumor control and overdosing leads to grade 3/4 neutropenia, neuropathy, and treatment discontinuation. For example, in mCRC, retrospective analysis of FOLFOX treatment has indicated < 30% of patients are administered what post hoc model suggests the optimally tolerated dose trajectory.

Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a principled approach to this sequential decision problem. The chemotherapy dosing is naturally expressed as a Markov decision process: in each cycle of treatment, clinician has access to state (blood counts, toxicity grades, biomarkers, performance status), and chooses action (dose, schedule or change agent), and receives a reward reflecting balance between tumor response and cumulative toxicity. Proof of concept studies by Zhao et al (2011) initially showed that an RL agent (with fully observable state) trained with simulated patient data could outperform fixed protocols in a compartment model myelosuppression. Recent applications of offline RL techniques (conservative Q-learning, behavioral cloned policy constraints, doubly robust off-policy evaluation) enable training on observational EMR data without dangerous online exploration in vulnerable populations. 2022-2024 TempoRL and other chemo dose-optimization projects at institutions such as MD Anderson and Duke have started the process of translating these techniques into prospective evaluation.

There are substantial hurdles between benchmarks achieved in retrospective RL and translation into trial interventions for deployment. These challenges include partial observability of disease burden, non-stationarity of patient physiology across courses, conservative safety bounds, regulatory challenges given FDA guidance on adaptive trial designs and AI/ML based software as a medical device, etc. This paper aims to discuss the framing of the adaptive chemo dose problem as an RL problem. Review the methodological strengths and weaknesses of published methods. We propose a trial design (with off-policy confidence bounds and clinician-in-the-loop policy veto) as a necessary precursor to first-in-human evaluation.

Introduction
Chemotherapy dosing decisions are arguably the most important but least optimized aspect of oncology care. The standard-of-care dosing of cytotoxic drugs like 5-fluorouracil, carboplatin, or doxorubicin was mostly determined by population-based dose-finding studies in the 1980s-90s, often set at a fixed body-surface-area-normalized dose with protocol-based toxicities prompting mandatory dose reductions. This blanket approach fails to account for the large inter-and intra-patient pharmacokinetic variability (often >10 fold changes in drug clearance) that is typical for cytotoxic drug delivery. As has been well-documented, under-dosing leads to inadequate tumor control while over-dosing leads to grade 3-4 neutropenia/neuropathy and treatment discontinuation. In the setting of mCRC, for instance, retrospective studies of FOLFOX administration have shown that less than 30% of patients appear to have received the (post hoc modeling of) optimal dose tolerance level.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is a principled approach to the sequential decision problem of chemotherapy dosing. Specifically, the chemotherapy dosing problem can be easily modeled as a Markov Decision Process where the clinician makes a dosing decision (e.g., dose level, timing, or change in drug) in each treatment cycle based on a state (e.g., blood counts, toxicity grade, biomarkers, performance status) and receives a reward that depends on a balance between tumor response and cumulative toxicity. Initial proof of concept studies by Zhao et al. (2011) showed that a fully observable RL agent could indeed be trained from simulated patient data to perform better than fixed protocols in a compartmentalized model of myelosuppression. Recently, offline RL approaches (conservative Q-learning, policy constraint via behavior cloning, and doubly robust off-policy evaluation) have also allowed learning from observational (e.g., EHR) data without the need for (risk of) unsafe online exploration in vulnerable patient populations. Institutions like MD Anderson and Duke have recently started (in 2022-2024TempoRL and others) to move towards prospective evaluation of these approaches for dose optimization.

However, there are substantial challenges between the retrospective RL evaluation benchmarks and actual deployment as a trial intervention. Partial observability of disease burden, non-stationary patient physiology during treatment courses, conservative safety constraints and regulatory uncertainty (under FDA adaptive trial design and AI/ML based software as medical device guidance) all pose major challenges. Here, we provide a review of the formulation of adaptive chemo-dosing as a RL problem, review the methodological strengths and weaknesses of the published work, and outline a trial design (including off-policy confidence bounds and clinician in the loop policy veto) which we believe is a necessary prerequisite for first-in-human evaluation.

I stayed at the Marriott City Center in downtown Denver (1717 Champa St) Sept 17-20.  I reserved online with them and it was $280/night.  They also have this funky destination fee that's $32 that's not obvious when you checkout.  The total (including tax) was a little over $1,050 for 3 nights. 
 
The room I had was a basic king room.  It was on the 12th floor.  I had a pretty good view of the 16th street mall construction (still under construction, it'll probably never be done).  The bed was really really nice!  I actually slept better than my bed at home.  Air conditioning was good.  It was still 85 degrees or so in the day.

The killer here is the parking.  $52/night for valet.  No option to self park in the hotel.  The closest garage (2 blocks away) was $28/night.

Got laid off from teaching in August. Here's what I learned from the first 60 days 
 Two days before inservice week was scheduled to begin (August 12) I received a phone call from my principal at Jefferson Elementary to inform me that my position was being "eliminated due to low enrollment." All 6 years of 4th grade teaching would be coming to an end over the course of a 4 minute phone call. 
 This isn't a pity post. It's to share that the past two months have been a crash course in learning. I wish someone had given me this info at the start. 
 
 Unemployment paperwork is a part time job. It was three weeks and two denied applications until I realized that I had put my last day of work in wrong. File quickly and make sure you quadruple check. First unemployment check I received September 19th. 
 Your teaching skills are more useful than you think. Employers don't know this. I was applying to "training" jobs and "instructional design" jobs. No response. The second I changed my resume from "I taught 4th grade" to "I managed 28 person team. Presented 6 hours a day. Analyzed performance data." - I had 4 interviews in two weeks. Monday the 14th I'll be starting a customer success role at a software company in Cedar Rapids. Not teaching. Getting an additional $9k over district 
 Weird and real grief. Cried in Target school supplies on August 20th. Didn't see that coming. Allow for the grief moments. 
 People want to help but you need to ask. A former parent learned about my layoff and put me in touch with company who ultimately hired me. Would've never found this job on Indeed 
 If you're a teacher still in the classroom who's worried about job security... start updating your resume now. Not when you get the phone call. 
 If you have questions I'm happy to answer in the comments. Jefferson people - I miss you guys!

 For the next two weeks, people are texting me with bees in a chimney on Oak street, bees in a mail box on Franklin Ave, bees hanging on the playground fence near Lincoln elementary.  For some reason, people are under the assumption that I know what to do. 
 I don't.  I've probably watched about 4 youtube videos. 
 But I get myself a veil.  Borrow Dennis' smoker.  I start reaching out to real beekeepers.  Come August I've helped coordinate the removal of 11 swarms.  Including one in the ceiling of our town library.  Librarian gives me a thank you card signed by all the staff.  My 7 year old daughter now calls me the "bee lady".  (Yet I'm a guy named Mark) 
 Here's the crazy thing...  people are still calling me.  Just last month I get a voice mail message saying "suspicious humming by the courthouse". 
 I'm not a beekeeper.  I've never had a hive.  I just happened to pick up the phone in 2021. 
 AITA if I just stop answering and let these actual professionals deal with these suspicious bees at the courthouse?

1 Year / 15,000 Miles - 2023 Model Y. Honest Review. (the $600 pain in the ass). 
 
Purchased my long range model y in March of 2023. Costa Mesa ca delivery center. Thought 1 year would be a good point to do a non honey moon phase review. 
 
Pros: Acceleration still puts a smile on my face daily. It's like comparing a Honda CRV 2018 to my Y. I'm at roughly $11 to fill up on 240V at home vs $70+ pump gas. Superchargers are pretty amazing. I went to Phoenix in January and I never worried about range. Autopilot is a god send during traffic on the 5 freeway. 
 
Cons: still can see the panel gaps on rear driver side. The wipers still confuse themselves at times. Sentry Mode does impact the battery a lot. How about no physical blind spot indicator? That's a big pet peeve. Also had 2 incidents of phantom braking on the I10. Scary both times. 
 
$600 fix. In November my touch screen started to randomly reboot while driving. Brought it to Costa Mesa service center. They had it for 4 days and determined it was an mcu4 connector issue. Covered?  NO. Because I had aftermarket dash cam installed by 3rd party shop in sept. They said voltage interference. Had to pay $612. It could be true or just an excuse. I'll never know. 
 
Rating: 8/10. Drive and savings are there. But build quality / service accountability doesn't let it be higher. Would I buy again? Probably. But no aftermarket electronics.

Report Period: Year 2 Q3 (July 1 - Sept 21, 2026)
PI: Dr. Rachel Ostrander, Department of Materials Science, Purdue University

Summary: The award "Scalable Synthesis of Anisotropic Nanocomposites for Low-Energy Thermal Regulation" has completed 3 out of 5 milestones for Year 2 of the grant.

Milestone 1 (Scale-up Reactor Completion, May 2026): 5-liter continuous flow reactor successfully commissioned at West Lafayette lab. 92% yield consistency in 40 batch processes, surpassing 85% goal.

Milestone 2 (Anisotropic Alignment Method, July 2026): Developed by graduate student Wei Chen. Magnetic field enhanced alignment protocol produced 0.87 order parameter. Publication in Advanced Materials Interfaces (August 2026).

Milestone 3 (Thermal Conductivity Benchmark, Sept 15, 2026): Postdoc Dr. Amara Osei completed benchmarking against 12 commercial composites at Argonne CNM lab. Confirms 34% drop in crossplane thermal conductivity vs. isotropic.

In progress: Milestone 4 (Durability testing with 500 cycles). 60% complete, full data set expected by Dec. 2026

Milestone 5 (Integration to prototype thermal barrier device). Not yet begun. Device housing availability confirmed by fabrication partner Sandia National Lab. (Jan 2027).

Field Work Log: Bird Count Cedar Swamp
Week of May 6-15 2024
Submitted By: Dana Whitfield Field Tech. Northline Audubon Society

Summary of Field Activity
In 10 continuous days of surveying (team of 3: D. Whitfield, M. Okafor, and intern J. Reyes) we conducted 40 point counts within the Cedar Swamp monitoring grid (all 8 established stations). Morning (0530-0900hrs) and evening (1700-1930hrs). For the most part, favorable weather except for May 9 morning point count, shortened by heavy rains.

Results
Total of 42 species (we counted 37 in same period last year)
Total Individuals: 1,184

Interesting results / notables:
Virginia rail: (Detected 4X station 3. Could be breeding pair, last confirmed 2019)
Prothonotary warbler: 1 male singing station 6 on May 11, 13 - note to check nest boxes.
Great blue heron: Activity in rookery (North dike) at least 6 occupied nests.
Common (sparrow), and yellowthroat again were top species. Approximately 22% of total observations.

The stations with highest abundances were 3 and 6 (38% of total observations). This is probably a response to the additional emergent marsh as a result of last fall's hydrology restoration.

Data input into eBird is complete. Internal (Northline) data base is also complete.
Note: Review of audio recordings of autonomous recording units (ARU's) station 2, 7 (J. Reyes to complete by 5/22)

Issues and Recommendations
1) Boardwalk (4-5) deteriorating, 2 planks loose, recommend maintenance before June survey round.
2) Heavy mosquitos this year. Suggest bring repellent for final spring surveys.
3) After warbler note: Suggest 2 nest boxes be installed close to station 6 before June 1.

Next Steps:
Next survey round will be June 3-12
We will distribute team assignment by 5/27

Please contact me (d.whitfield@northlineaudubon.org) for any questions.

Field Research Log: bird populations count - Cedar Swamp Week of May 6-15, 2024 Submitted by: Dana Whitfield, Field Technician, Northline Audubon Society

Activity Summary

Reyes) conducted 40 point counts within Cedar Swamp monitoring grid (all 8 established stations during both morning 0530 - 0900 and evening 1700 - 1930). For the most part we had decent weather, aside from the morning of 05/09 where heavy rains cut our count short.

Results
Species: 42 in total (vs 37 for the same time last year).

Total individuals: 1,184 Notable and highlights:

Last confirmed sighting 2019.

Next survey period 06/03 - 06/12.

Elevator 3 (Tower B floors 1 - 14) was placed out of service on Wednesday, Feb 12 at 7:45 AM due to sporadic door close faults and tenants on 9th floor reporting a hard stop. Facilities Technician Raymond Ortiz ran initial diagnostics that afternoon and discovered that it appears worn out door interlock contacts and a worn main drive sheave bearing were most likely the causes of the elevator's issues.

Service Call was logged with Almeida Elevator Co. on the same day. Testing (Full run load tests, 50 Door cycles) were conducted on Feb 18-19 by elevator technician Dana Whitfield and Facilities Technician Raymond Ortiz. ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Trattoria Roma... carbonara love  

My sis and I went to Trattoria Roma on a rainy Friday (March 14) around 7:30pm after a Cubs game. Had 25 min wait quoted but we got seated sooner than that (like 15min) which is great for a Friday! The place is cute with exposed brick, good lighting, slightly loud (but good vibe - not 'can't hear each other' loud).  

But the main reason I'm reviewing this is... THE CARBONARA!! Yeah, it's on the high side for the area at $19.95... But the carbonara did it for me. Clearly the pasta was made in-house (texture can tell) and it was slightly over al-dente (but some purists may complain. And whatever! Lol). The sauce was nice and smooth. Nothing cream was involved. Just eggs yolk. Pecorino. Rendered guilt (guanciale, man). The pork were in nice chunks, crispy edges and all. Not the sad bacon shreds u get from some places. Nice ground black pepper also. Lotsa bite. The portion size was good. I could not finish it. I rarely say that.  

Attentive service. Not overbearing. Our server was Daniela. She came to us at the right time. Water glasses were refilled. We got a bread basket with the herby olive oil dip. We obliterated that waiting for our order.  

The in-house Chianti ($9/glass) was a tad watery. Table also wobbly but Daniela helped fold napkin under the leg to fix it. Ha ha!  Street parking also crazy in that area. So valet up.  

Total was $78 (w/ a tiramisu which was great. Real espresso bite.) (for two. Drinks included.) Before tip. Worth it. Will go back for cacio e pepe.

Purchased Anker Power bank 313 (PowerCore 20K / 20000mAh) from amazon for $39.99 in May (shipped on May 14). This was purchased with the intention of having it as a reliable power supply for a two week trip in Portugal in June. During the first 3 months it worked as intended, able to fully charge my pixel 8 and still have 60% of the charge left in the power bank. 
 
 In early September it started losing power really fast. It will have 3 bars on the LED indicator. I will plug in my phone. It will quickly drop to 1 bar within 10 minutes of charging my phone. By mid September it will not hold a charge overnight. I will charge it to 100% before going to sleep. I will unplug it. In the morning it will read empty. No phone has been plugged into it. I've tried it with 3 different USB-C cables and 2 different wall adapters. So not a cable issue. 
 
 I reached out to Anker via their site on Sept 18th with my order number. They asked for video of the led behavior. I sent it the following day. As of today 9/21 I have yet to hear from them with a replacement. That's 3 days with no response. 
 
 I was expecting a bit more than 4 months out of a $40 power bank. While the quality and the charging speed was very good when it worked. Anker has a 18 month warranty. That's the only reason I'm not just tossing this to the side. I'll update this review if Anker support helps me out with a replacement. But for now I can't recommend this particular one until I know how it's handled.

review_product_05_luna.text:
The Midnight Library by Matt Haig. Nora Seed is a 35 year old in Bedford who is neither dead nor alive after attempting to take her own life. At a mysterious library led by her former librarian, Mrs Elm, she looks through different versions of her life through books that describe the options she could have chosen (swimming in the Olympics, managing a pub in Australia, marrying Dan, learning about glaciers)

It's a fascinating concept and Matt Haig is very kind and accessible in the way he deals with Nora's depression. I especially appreciated the main concept of the library: regrets make us believe we could fix everything with the right choice, but there are always problems in every life. The chapters are short and easy to read. Specifics about swimming, music, chess and the Arctic add a rich (almost dreamy) sense to the options available to Nora.

But sometimes there is a little too much telling about the message. Some of the insights that Nora has are a bit like inspirational quotes rather than things she has learned through living. Also, I was a little let down by the end. It's very positive and I can see why the author would want Nora to feel like she has a lot of options at the end, but it feels a bit quick and tidy after all the darkness at the beginning of the book. And it's a bit too fast that Nora goes back to her life. The complexity of mental health issues is a little simplified to the message that we should decide to live.

But it's a kind and creative book that is quite easy to be emotionally invested in. Not every philosophical point is subtle but I was struck by the experience of Nora. In particular the idea that there are a lot of options in even what seems a normal life.

Nora Seed is a 35 year old Bedford woman. The Midnight Library is about Nora being suspended between life and death after attempting suicide. In a strange library guided by her old school librarian Mrs Elm, Nora experiences different lives by opening up books of the choices she might have made. What if she became an Olympic swimmer? What if she owned a pub in Australia? What if she married Dan? What if she studied glaciology?

It's an interesting concept right away. Matt Haig does a good job of presenting Nora's depression in an understandable and relatable way. In particular I enjoyed the concept of the library and that we tend to think that there's just one decision that would be perfect and solve all our regrets, but every life has its problems. The chapters are short and easy to read. There's a lot of interesting details around swimming, music, chess and the Arctic etc. that makes it seem almost dreamlike with all the possibilities for Nora.

However there are moments where it feels like it makes too much effort to explain its message. Some of the 'realisations' Nora comes to seem like more like inspirational quotes than 'a-ha' moments of discovery. I was a little let down by the end as well. It's positive, and I can see why Matt Haig wants to make sure Nora has a clear idea of possibility. But it just feels a bit rushed and tidy after all the heavy emotional atmosphere at the start of the book. The way Nora comes back to her original life is so fast that it does kind of smooth over the complexity of her mental health issues a little in favour of just the lesson that you should decide to live.

But overall it's a caring, imaginative book that draws you in emotionally. I didn't always think it was subtle in the philosophical ideas, but I do like Nora's journey and the idea that a 'normal' life has so much potential that we aren't aware of.

review_product_07_glm.text:
Just finished a 3000 mile trip (Portland, OR down to San Diego and back) in my 2022 Toyota RAV4 Hybrid and WOW. 
 I'm impressed enough to write a review! 
 Average mpg for the trip? 39.8! Yes, that's hand calculated over 9 fillups. Not just the dash (which was 1mpg optimistic). 
 Toyota advertises 40 mpg combined. 
 On flat highways through the central valley I could see 42-43 at 70mph. 
 Passes in the mountains by Grants pass and Grapevine dropped me to ~34mpg. But hey, I expected that. 
 2.5L Hybrid is...smooth. Not exciting. 
 You have to plan ahead for merging onto I5. 219hp is plenty. But not exciting. Also the CVT drones when you punch it. But that's not why you buy this car. 
 Comfort: wow. After 500 miles days, my back (and my wife's) were fine. Seats were good. 
 Road noise was ok. (quieter than the gas only Rav4 I test drove in 2021) 
 The back could handle 2 duffel bags, cooler and dog crate with room to spare. 
 Wish the infotainment screen wasn't from last decade. 
 Lane keeping assist on XLE trim constantly bugged us when driving the windy highway 101. So we just turned it off. 
 Also the brakes feel a little grippy in the first few inches of travel. Which is typical of Toyota hybrids. Just takes a few hundred miles to get used to. 
 Total fuel used for trip. ~75 gal. ~340$  considering California / Oregon gas prices. 
 vs. Something similar in a gas SUV...would've been almost double that. 
 Would I buy it again? Sure. Great vehicle for road tripping, fuel economy, haul stuff. And just needs oil changes.

Just got a Logitech M240 Silent (24.99$ @best buy <checkout sept 2nd> to replace an mx anywhere 3 (79.99$). I have been using the mx3 for the last 2 years as my daily driver. After 3 weeks here is what I can say about it. Save 55$ if you are most people. 
 It only connects via bluetooth, no logi bolt receiver. It took 4 sec for it to connect to my M2 macbook air. The scrolling is not the hyperfast free spinning wheel of the mx, it is a basic notchy scroll. So if you need to scroll through a 2k row spreadsheet it will take longer. The side buttons. There are 2 of them. Same as the mx. And yes you can remap it all in logi options+. The sensor has a max DPI of 4000. The mx anywhere 3 has a max DPI of 8000. I never felt a difference on a desk but when I use it on my lap and use my knee as a mousepad. It would skip a bit sometimes. 
 Advantages of the M240. 
 It has a 18month battery life according to logitech. Using one AA battery. I am 1 month in and the app still says 100% battery life. MX has a usb c to charge. And I have to charge it every 2-3 months when I use it regularly. The M240 is 15g lighter (78g vs 99g). So if you are taking it to the coffee shop everyday like me it matters. 
 The construction feels less solid, it sounds hollow clickier. There is a seam on the bottom. But the clicks are quieter, so that is nice for when you are on calls. 
 So if you are just connecting to one machine. Don't need to change between devices. (The mx anywhere 3 can switch 3 devices with logi bolt or bluetooth. And all you need to do is press a button. ) The m240 will get you 90% of your daily usage. For 1/3 the price. So I will be using the m240 when I travel. And the mx for my desk set up.

Not a big fan of roguelikes as it's more of a pain than it is fun to run the same levels over and over once you die. But *Hades* sure is something different. 
 Been playing on the Nintendo Switch since March 2024. I thought I'll stop after a few attempts but ended up playing a good 35 hours just to escape the Underworld as Zagreus. 
 The action is pretty fast but simple - dash, attack, cast, different boons each run. 1/ In November of 2021 I closed down my first startup: **RelayCart** after 18 months of building. $120k raised. 47 paying customers. Still couldn't turn it into a sustainable business.

2/ [Lesson 1] You can have a very real problem that is not urgent. The inventory dashboard for small retailers was cool. Few were ready to alter their process and pay for it.

3/ [Lesson 2] Only revenue is compounding validation. All the accolades, waitlists, 'I'd def use this!' comments weren't enough to pay the team.

4/ [Lesson 3] We had too much staff too soon. By March of 2021 we had a 4-person team burning through $14k/month before PMF.

5/ [Lesson 4] Meet with customers every week. Too much time building in Oakland. Not enough time meeting with (the store owners) we claimed to be building for.

6/ [Lesson 5] Alignment for cofounders is key. My cofounder wanted to raise funds. I wanted to focus on profitability. We didn't tackle this until it was too late.

7/ [Lesson 6] Have kill criteria. We should have stopped by 6 months of being under $5k MRR, not when the bank account hit $8,300

8/ [Lesson 7] Failure is a costly lesson. But only if you take time to learn from it. I'm building less quickly now. Selling sooner. Tracking behavior vs interest.

1/ In November 2021, I closed my first startup called **RelayCart** after 18 months. We got $120k raised, 47 paying customers... and we couldn't sustain it.

2/ 1. You can have a "real" problem but not a "pressing" one. Small retailers wanted our inventory dashboard. But they weren't going to change habits much. And were reluctant to pay.

3/ 2. Only revenue compounds as validation. It's great to hear kind words. To get waitlists. And get "I'd definitely use this" comments. But it's not going to pay your payroll.

4/ 3. You probably shouldn't have hired that early. By March 2021, we had 4 people on the team. Burning $14k/mo before getting a product-market fit.

5/ 4. Talk to your customers weekly. I spent too much time working on it here in Oakland. Not enough time in front of store owners we said we helped.

6/ 5. Co-founder alignment is crucial. My co-founder wanted to do fundraising. I wanted to be profitable. We kept it from bursting at the seams... until we couldn't.

7/ 6. Have "kill" criteria. We should've killed the project at 6 months of being under $5k MRR. Not when bank account is at $8,300.

8/ 7. Failures are lessons that cost you a lot. But only if you learn from them. Now I'm iterating slower, selling faster, measuring actions not enthusiasm.

1/3 Cold emailed 200 VCs for my seed round. Spr. 2024 5 painful lessons learned.

"Hey we're the future of collaboration!"

Nope, not resonating with a NY fintech investor or Boston healthcare investor.

❌Mistake 2. Highlighted product features over traction.

Our best proof was $18,400 MRR and 37% MOM growth in March.

2/3 ❌Mistake 3. Some of these partners NEVER invest at seed stage.

Some had $500M+ funds, but they wrote their first check at Series A.

Should've dug into their websites and recent investments before I hit 'send'.

❌Mistake 4. My ask was, "15min to connect."

Should've been a clear and specific ask:

"Would you be interested in leading a $1.5M seed round for a B2B workflow tool. It's growing 37% MOM"

3/3 ❌Mistake 5. Followed up emotionally and unconsistently

4 emails in 10 days for some VCs.

No follow up beyond initial email to some VCs.

The system I eventually landed on was this:

3 intentional follow ups over 21 days. Every one has a new data point.

We raised in July 2024.

Cold email isn't just about volume. It's about relevance.

Proof.

Timing.

1/3 Cold-emailing 200 VCs for my seed round this spring gave me 5 painful lessons.

1) My big mistake #1 was sending one generic pitch to all of them. "Hey, we're working on the future of collaboration" was irrelevant if you were a fintech investor in NYC or a healthcare investor in Boston.

2) My mistake #2 was focusing on product features not traction. The best proof we had was $18,400 MRR and 37% MoM growth in March. I had it on slide 12.

2/3 3) My mistake #3 was sending partners who never do seed deals. Some had $500M+ funds and their first check was a Series A. I should have checked their site and their recent deals before sending the email.

4) My mistake #4 was asking for "15 minutes to connect" instead of a clear specific ask. "Would you be interested in leading a $1.5M seed round for a B2B workflow tool that's growing 37% MoM?".

3/3 5) My mistake #5 was doing an emotional and inconsistent follow up. Some VCs got 4 emails from me in 10 days. Others got 0 after first email. Eventually what I found was 3 thoughtful follow-up emails over 21 days. Each one with new data point.

We ended up closing the round in July 2024. Biggest lesson is cold emailing isn't just a volume game. More important is relevance, proof, timing over 200 emails.

Career change from civil engineering (19 yrs) to data analyst @age 43. Here's what I found. 
 I knew last March after the stormwater drainage project for the city of Mesa that I was uncomfortable with the truth. My favorite thing about my job wasn't designing infrastructure. It was creating excel models and dashboards to help with project budgets. 
 So I decided what to do. 14 months of evenings/weekends. Google Data Analytics Certificate. Then SQL on DataCamp. Then Python. I ended up finishing 3 portfolio projects. One of those was me taking my old domain knowledge and using it with the new skills to determine predictive maintenance of drainage systems (analysing rainfall data for 12 yrs in AZ). 
 I finally got a data analyst role in May at a phoenix logistics company. I took a 12% pay cut for the first year. I'm making more than I did as a Sr. Civil Engineer after 6 months. 
 The thing they don't tell you when you're thinking about changing careers. 
 1. Your old skills aren't bad. They're good. The fact that I had engineering experience made me more equipped to ask questions and interpret operational data than a bootcamp grad who had no context for the industry. 
 2. Your age is your friend. 20 years of communicating with stakeholders, meeting deadlines, knowing how businesses actually operate. You can't get that at a bootcamp. 
 3. It's not too late. It's also not free. I sacrificed 14 months of weekends. That's the cost. 
 This is your sign if you're on the fence (3 years for me). 
 #careerchange #dataanalytics #careerpivot #nevertoolate

zh_essay_01_sonnet.text:
2023年初，ChatGPT在全球大学范围内引发了一波小小的地震。据国外媒体报道，美国斯坦福大学的调查结果显示，超过17%的学生承认自己会在期末的论文中辅助使用ChatGPT。香港大学甚至一度直接禁止学生在未授权的情况下使用ChatGPT来完成作业或论文，但之后在争议声中又撤销了相关禁令。国内高校也是迅速作出应对，如复旦大学、天津大学等相继出台政策要求学生在论文中表述是否使用生成式AI工具等。围绕着"谁来写一篇论文"的讨论，直接把大学写作教育中的一个难题暴露在阳光下：论文写作的边界是什么？

论文的边界，不应该在"是否使用工具"这个位置，而应该在"是否发生思维"这个位置。论文写作的本质，从来不仅仅是写出一篇连贯的文字，而是一个完整的问题提出-文献检索-证据辨别-论述组织-迭代修改的过程，涉及到的思维活动。虽然ChatGPT可以在几秒钟内写出一篇逻辑清晰语言连贯的文字，但它代替不了学生对于一手材料的思考与选择。如果学生简单地把题目甩给它，复制粘贴完事，那不管多先进的技术，也不是"论文写作"，而变成了"代笔"，和请人写论文本质上是一样的。相反，如果学生使用它来梳理文献脉络，进行逻辑检查，修饰语言，同时保持自己对于材料的独立思考和核心观点的陈述，那与使用工具书、询问老师、使用语法检测软件本质上没什么区别，也不应该一概斥之为学术不端行为。

但这个边界本身又很难在实践中量化和监管。我曾经听到北京大学某一位从事写作教学的老师在校内讨论时说，当前的查重工具只是对于文字的重复进行检测，并不能对于一段论述是否经过学生思考进行判断，所以"是否使用AI"变得像是无从检验的"良心"问题。更加现实的情况是，很多课程的评价标准还是"文字是否流畅，格式是否规范"这种，刚好又是ChatGPT最容易伪装的点，但不是我们写作教育真正想要评判的地方。

与其纠结于"是否可以使用工具"这样的问题，还不如着力于改进写作训练本身。比如要求学生提供写作过程稿、论点口头答辩、以课堂讨论为基础的分析等等。把评价的重点从结果转向思维可追溯性。技术的发展是不可避免的，下一波会引起争议的工具很快就会出现。但只要我们教育者坚持"独立思考不可代劳"的底线，论文写作的边界就是很清楚的。工具可以帮助你将文字更好地表达，但不能替你决定说什么。

zh_essay_01_sonnet.text:
2023年ChatGPT引起世界高校的小小地震，国外媒体报道，美国斯坦福大学对学生进行调查，结果有超过17%的学生自述在期末论文写作中使用了ChatGPT。香港大学曾叫停学生未经授权使用ChatGPT写作业论文，后在争议中解除禁令。国内高校也反应迅速，复旦、天津大学等高校相继出台要求，学生论文要注明是否使用生成式AI工具。这场“论文由谁来写”的讨论其实直接戳到了大学写作教育的死穴。关于“论文写作到底在什么位置的边界”的问题一直悬而未解。

在我看来，“是否使用工具”并不是边界所在，而是“是否有思维产生”才是个边界。写论文不是单纯的产出文字，而是一个思考问题、检索文献、甄别证据、构建论述、修正的整个思维过程。ChatGPT几秒钟就可以搞出一段流畅连贯的论述，但却无法取代学生对于一手材料的取舍与判断。如果学生把题目交给AI，复制粘贴交差就完事儿了。不管技术多么高精尖，这都不是论文写作了。这是代笔，和找人代写并没有本质区别。但如果学生利用它梳理文献思路，检查逻辑漏洞，润色语言。同时保持自己对材料的分析和核心论点。这和查工具书、请教老师、用语法软件检查并没有太大区别，不应该被视为学术不端。

但这条边界难以量化，难以监督。一位北大师范授课的老师在学校的讨论中说过，现在的查重只能识别文字重复，并不能判定某段论述是否经过学生思考。所以“是否使用AI”几乎成了一个无法监督的良心题。还有一个困境是评价的滞后，不少课程评分还是基于“文字流畅程度，格式规整程度”这些内容为主。而这些恰好是ChatGPT伪装最成功的，但不是写作教育想要培养的。

所以，不要纠结于“能否使用工具”。我们可以把精力投入到重新设计写作练习之中。如要求提交写作过程稿，口头答辩观点。基于课堂讨论的分析等。评价重点转而从最终文字变为对思维可追溯性。技术总是会升级的，下一个惹麻烦的工具也很快会出现。但教育者只要守住“独立思考不能外包”的底线。论文写作的边界很清楚的。工具可以帮助你更好的表达，但不能帮你决定说什么。

而忽略背后的成本。

有生命力的书店，是要大家来买书的。
